1: This course equips students with practical Python programming skills essential for data science applications in business environments. Students learn core Python libraries including NumPy, Pandas, and Scikit-learn for data manipulation, analysis, and machine learning model development. The course covers object-oriented programming principles, data structures, and functional programming paradigms relevant to professional data science workflows. Through hands-on projects, students develop proficiency in writing efficient, maintainable code for data processing pipelines, exploratory data analysis, and predictive modeling tasks. Upon completion, students can implement end-to-end data science solutions using Python and integrate them into business intelligence systems.
2: This course equips students with frameworks and methodologies for developing data-driven strategic plans in business contexts. Students learn to conduct competitive analysis, market assessment, and scenario planning using quantitative tools and business intelligence platforms. The course covers strategic decision-making models, balanced scorecard development, and key performance indicator (KPI) design, with emphasis on translating data insights into actionable business strategies. Through case studies and real-world projects, students practice formulating long-term organizational objectives, resource allocation strategies, and performance monitoring systems. Upon completion, students are able to synthesize complex business data into comprehensive strategic recommendations and communicate strategic initiatives to executive stakeholders.
3: This course equips students with advanced mathematical foundations essential for data analysis and statistical modeling in business contexts. Students study linear algebra, multivariate calculus, probability theory, and optimization techniques, with emphasis on their practical applications in machine learning and predictive analytics. The course covers matrix operations, eigenvalue decomposition, gradient descent algorithms, and Bayesian inference, utilizing computational tools such as Python and R for implementation. Students develop proficiency in formulating business problems as mathematical models and solving them using numerical methods and statistical algorithms. By course completion, students can apply sophisticated mathematical techniques to extract insights from complex datasets and validate analytical solutions in real-world business scenarios.
4: This course provides data scientists with rigorous mathematical foundations essential for advanced analytics and machine learning applications in business contexts. Students study probability theory, statistical distributions, linear algebra, calculus, and optimization techniques, with emphasis on their practical applications in data modeling and inference. The course covers probability spaces, conditional probability, Bayes' theorem, expectation and variance, and multivariate distributions, alongside matrix operations, eigenvalue decomposition, and gradient-based optimization methods. Through problem sets and computational exercises using Python and R, students develop proficiency in mathematical reasoning and learn to implement theoretical concepts for solving real-world business analytics problems. Upon completion, students can formulate probabilistic models, perform mathematical derivations for machine learning algorithms, and apply optimization techniques to business decision-making scenarios.
5: This course examines the intersection of business process management and data visualization techniques within organizational contexts. Students learn to map, analyze, and optimize business workflows while developing proficiency in visualization tools such as Tableau, Power BI, and Python libraries (Matplotlib, Seaborn, Plotly) to communicate complex data insights to stakeholders. The course covers process mining methodologies, key performance indicator (KPI) design, and dashboard development for real-time business monitoring. Students apply these skills to real-world case studies, creating interactive visualizations that support data-driven decision-making across functional business areas. Upon completion, students can design end-to-end business process improvements informed by data analytics and present findings through compelling visual narratives.
6: This course provides students with comprehensive knowledge of relational and non-relational database systems essential for business data management. Students learn database design principles, normalization techniques, SQL query optimization, and data modeling using entity-relationship diagrams and dimensional modeling approaches. The course covers practical implementation using PostgreSQL and NoSQL databases (MongoDB), enabling students to design scalable schemas and write efficient queries for business analytics. Students develop proficiency in data warehousing concepts, ETL processes, and indexing strategies to support decision-making systems. By course completion, students can architect databases for business applications, optimize query performance, and implement data governance practices in enterprise environments.
7: This course equips students with practical techniques and algorithms for extracting actionable insights from large datasets. Students learn supervised and unsupervised learning methods, including classification, clustering, regression, and association rule mining, alongside their business applications. The course covers data preprocessing, feature engineering, model evaluation, and interpretation of results using industry-standard tools such as Python, R, and SQL. Students develop proficiency in implementing mining algorithms on real-world business datasets and communicating findings to non-technical stakeholders. By course completion, students can design and execute complete data mining projects that drive strategic business decisions.
8: This course provides students with comprehensive training in machine learning algorithms and their practical applications in business contexts. Students learn supervised learning techniques including regression, classification, and ensemble methods, alongside unsupervised learning approaches such as clustering and dimensionality reduction. The course covers model evaluation, hyperparameter tuning, and validation strategies essential for building robust predictive systems. Students gain hands-on experience implementing machine learning pipelines using Python libraries such as scikit-learn, TensorFlow, and pandas, and apply these skills to real-world business datasets. Upon completion, students are able to develop, evaluate, and deploy machine learning models that solve business problems and drive data-informed decision-making.
9: This course provides students with comprehensive training in neural network architectures and deep learning methodologies for business applications. Students learn to design, implement, and optimize various neural network models including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and transformer architectures using frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch. The course covers fundamental concepts including backpropagation, gradient descent optimization, regularization techniques, and hyperparameter tuning to address real-world business problems. Students develop practical skills in building predictive models for classification, regression, and sequence analysis tasks, with applications to customer behavior analysis, demand forecasting, and natural language processing. By course completion, students are able to implement end-to-end deep learning pipelines, evaluate model performance, and deploy neural network solutions for business intelligence and decision-making.
10: This course covers the design, architecture, and implementation of data warehouses and ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) pipelines essential for enterprise data management. Students learn dimensional modeling, schema design patterns (star and snowflake schemas), and best practices for organizing large-scale data repositories. The course provides hands-on experience with industry-standard tools such as Apache Spark, Apache Airflow, and cloud-based data warehouse platforms (Snowflake, BigQuery, or Redshift) for building automated data pipelines. Students develop proficiency in data quality assurance, pipeline orchestration, and performance optimization techniques. By course completion, students can architect scalable data warehouse solutions, design and deploy production-grade ETL pipelines, and implement monitoring systems for data pipeline reliability in business environments.
11: This course explores the practical implementation and deployment of large language models (LLMs) in business contexts. Students learn to fine-tune pre-trained models, integrate LLMs into production systems, and evaluate model performance using domain-specific metrics. The course covers prompt engineering techniques, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and cost-optimization strategies for enterprise applications. Students work with frameworks such as LangChain and Hugging Face to build chatbots, recommendation systems, and automated content generation pipelines. By course completion, students can architect end-to-end LLM solutions that address real business problems while managing computational resources and ethical considerations.
12: This course examines the architecture and implementation of distributed systems essential for large-scale data processing and storage. Students learn fundamental concepts including consistency models, fault tolerance, replication, and partitioning strategies while studying systems such as Apache Hadoop, Spark, and Kafka. The course covers distributed computing frameworks, data pipeline orchestration, and techniques for managing data across multiple nodes in production environments. Through hands-on projects, students develop proficiency in designing scalable data architectures, optimizing data workflows, and troubleshooting distributed system failures. Upon completion, students can architect and deploy distributed data solutions that handle real-world enterprise data engineering challenges.
13: This course equips students with theoretical foundations and practical skills in computer vision techniques for business applications. Students learn image processing fundamentals, feature extraction, object detection, and deep learning architectures including CNNs, working with libraries such as OpenCV and TensorFlow. The course covers real-world use cases including quality control, document analysis, and visual recognition systems relevant to enterprise environments. Through hands-on projects, students develop the ability to design and implement computer vision pipelines that solve specific business problems and integrate vision models into production systems.
14: This course equips students with practical knowledge of cloud infrastructure management and cybersecurity principles essential for enterprise data science operations. Students learn to design, deploy, and maintain secure cloud environments using major platforms such as AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, while implementing authentication, encryption, and access control mechanisms. The course covers infrastructure-as-code tools, containerization technologies, and monitoring systems to ensure data integrity and system reliability in production environments. Students develop competency in threat assessment, compliance frameworks (GDPR, HIPAA), and incident response protocols specific to data-driven organizations. Upon completion, students can architect secure cloud solutions, manage data pipelines with appropriate security controls, and implement governance policies for sensitive business information.
15: This course explores the practical implementation and deployment of generative models in business contexts, covering architectures such as GANs, VAEs, and transformer-based models. Students develop proficiency in fine-tuning pre-trained generative models, prompt engineering, and integrating large language models into business applications using frameworks like PyTorch and Hugging Face. The course emphasizes real-world use cases including synthetic data generation, content creation, recommendation systems, and automated decision-making pipelines. Students complete hands-on projects that demonstrate how to evaluate model outputs, manage computational resources, and address ethical considerations in generative AI deployment. Upon completion, students can architect and implement generative model solutions that address specific business problems while maintaining data quality and regulatory compliance.
16: This course covers the theoretical foundations and practical applications of Bayesian statistical methods for business analytics and decision-making. Students learn to formulate prior distributions, compute posterior distributions, and conduct Bayesian inference using both analytical and computational techniques including Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and variational inference. The course emphasizes Bayesian approaches to hypothesis testing, parameter estimation, and predictive modeling, with applications to business problems such as A/B testing, customer segmentation, and risk assessment. Students develop proficiency in implementing Bayesian models using Python libraries such as PyMC and Stan, and learn to interpret results in a business context. By course completion, students can construct custom Bayesian models, evaluate model performance through posterior predictive checks, and communicate uncertainty quantification to non-technical stakeholders.
17: This course examines the psychological, social, and economic factors that influence consumer decision-making and purchasing patterns. Students analyze behavioral data using statistical methods, machine learning algorithms, and data visualization tools to identify consumer segments, predict preferences, and model purchase intent. The course covers key frameworks including utility theory, prospect theory, and attribution models, with practical applications in market basket analysis, recommendation systems, and customer lifetime value prediction. Students apply these concepts to real-world datasets using Python, R, and business intelligence platforms to develop actionable insights for marketing strategy and product development. Upon completion, students can design data-driven consumer research studies, interpret behavioral analytics, and translate consumer insights into business recommendations.
18: This course equips data science students with econometric methods and time series analysis techniques essential for business forecasting and causal inference. Students learn classical regression frameworks, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences estimation, and advanced time series models including ARIMA, GARCH, and vector autoregression (VAR). The course emphasizes practical implementation using Python and R, with applications to real business datasets for demand forecasting, financial risk modeling, and policy evaluation. Students develop competency in diagnosing model assumptions, handling non-stationary data, and interpreting results for business decision-making. Upon completion, students can construct predictive models for temporal business data, conduct causal analysis from observational data, and communicate econometric findings to non-technical stakeholders.
19: This course examines distributed computing frameworks and technologies essential for processing large-scale datasets in business environments. Students learn the architecture and implementation of Apache Hadoop, Apache Spark, and related big data platforms, focusing on MapReduce programming models, data partitioning strategies, and cluster management. The course covers practical applications including data ingestion pipelines, batch processing, and real-time stream processing using tools such as Kafka and Spark Streaming. Students develop proficiency in writing scalable data processing jobs, optimizing query performance on distributed systems, and managing data warehouses for business analytics. By course completion, students can design and implement big data solutions that handle petabyte-scale datasets and support data-driven decision-making in enterprise contexts.
20: This course examines the intersection of technology innovation and business creation within the data science context. Students explore frameworks for identifying market opportunities, developing technology-driven business models, and building scalable data products from concept to commercialization. The course covers venture assessment methodologies, intellectual property protection, funding strategies, and go-to-market approaches specific to data-intensive startups. Through case studies and practical projects, students develop business plans for data science applications and learn to communicate technical innovations to investors and stakeholders. Upon completion, students will be able to evaluate technological feasibility and market viability of data science ventures and construct comprehensive business strategies for data-driven entrepreneurial initiatives.
21: This course equips data science students with essential economic principles and frameworks necessary for business analytics and decision-making. Students examine microeconomic and macroeconomic concepts, market structures, consumer behavior, and firm dynamics through a quantitative lens, with emphasis on applications relevant to business intelligence. The course covers econometric modeling, causal inference, and time series analysis using Python and R, enabling students to analyze economic data and forecast business trends. Students develop competency in interpreting economic indicators, evaluating business strategies through economic theory, and communicating findings to non-technical stakeholders. Upon completion, students can apply economic reasoning to real-world business problems and integrate economic insights into data-driven decision-making frameworks.

Participants work on authentic datasets and business cases, utilizing tools such as Python, SQL, and visualization platforms to deliver actionable insights. Upon completion, students demonstrate proficiency in translating business requirements into analytical solutions, communicating findings to non-technical stakeholders, and collaborating effectively within data science teams. 23: Students conduct original research on a data science application relevant to business contexts under faculty supervision. The thesis requires students to formulate a research question, design and execute a comprehensive analytical study, and present findings through written and oral defense. Students apply advanced statistical methods, machine learning techniques, and business analytics tools learned throughout the program to solve real-world problems in domains such as marketing analytics, financial forecasting, or operational optimization. The completed thesis demonstrates mastery of data science methodology, critical thinking, and the ability to communicate complex technical results to both technical and business audiences.

The course emphasizes reproducible research practices, statistical rigor, and the ethical implications of data science in organizational contexts. By completion, students are prepared to conduct independent research projects and contribute meaningfully to academic and professional discourse in data science.

Students apply computational tools to analyze environmental datasets and construct predictive models for ecological scenarios. Upon completion, students can evaluate environmental systems using mathematical frameworks and contribute to evidence-based environmental protection strategies.

30: This course examines the political, social, and cultural development of Armenia from ancient times through the medieval period. 59: This course extends foundational calculus concepts to multivariable functions and their applications. 68: This course covers fundamental numerical techniques for solving linear algebra problems that arise in scientific computing and engineering applications. 69: This course covers the theory and methods for solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs), fundamental to modeling dynamic systems in science and engineering. 70: This course covers fundamental and advanced concepts in graph theory, including graph representations, connectivity, paths, cycles, and tree structures. 120: This course covers fundamental algorithms and data structures for solving geometric problems computationally. 121: This course examines formal methods for specifying, verifying, and validating software systems with mathematical rigor. Students study temporal logics (LTL, CTL), model checking algorithms, theorem proving techniques, and formal specification languages such as Z and Alloy. The course covers automated verification tools, including SPIN and NuSMV, and their application to concurrent and reactive systems. Students develop proficiency in constructing formal proofs, detecting design flaws through exhaustive state-space exploration, and applying formal methods to real-world software engineering problems. Upon completion, students can formally specify complex systems, verify critical properties, and employ automated reasoning to ensure software correctness.
122: This course examines foundational and advanced concepts in artificial intelligence within the context of discrete mathematics and computational theory. Students study knowledge representation, logical reasoning systems, search algorithms, machine learning fundamentals, and natural language processing techniques. The course covers formal methods for problem-solving including constraint satisfaction, game theory, and automated reasoning, with emphasis on algorithmic complexity and theoretical soundness. Students implement AI systems using logic programming, symbolic reasoning frameworks, and classical machine learning algorithms, developing the ability to design and analyze intelligent systems grounded in discrete mathematical principles. Upon completion, students can formalize AI problems mathematically, select appropriate algorithmic approaches, and evaluate solution correctness and computational efficiency.
123: This course examines the mathematical foundations of information theory and its applications to data compression, communication systems, and cryptography. Students study entropy, mutual information, channel capacity, and the Shannon-Hartley theorem, developing rigorous proofs of fundamental limits on information transmission and storage. The course covers source coding theory, including Huffman and arithmetic coding algorithms, as well as channel coding techniques for error correction and detection. Students apply these concepts through computational projects involving data compression analysis, channel capacity calculations, and information-theoretic security evaluation. Upon completion, students can analyze information systems quantitatively, design efficient coding schemes, and apply information-theoretic principles to solve problems in telecommunications and data science.
124: This course examines formal systems for representing and reasoning about computational problems through logical frameworks. Students study propositional and first-order logic, resolution methods, and automated theorem proving techniques, with emphasis on their applications to program verification and knowledge representation. The course covers SAT solvers, constraint satisfaction problems, and logic programming paradigms such as Prolog. Through practical assignments, students implement logical inference engines and apply computational logic to solve problems in formal verification and symbolic computation. Upon completion, students can design logical specifications for systems, apply automated reasoning tools, and analyze the computational complexity of logical decision problems.
125: This course provides advanced study of combinatorial structures and counting techniques essential to theoretical computer science and discrete mathematics. Students explore permutations, combinations, generating functions, recurrence relations, and inclusion-exclusion principles, with applications to algorithm analysis and complexity theory. The course covers graph enumeration, partition theory, and combinatorial designs, emphasizing both classical results and modern computational approaches. Students develop proficiency in applying combinatorial methods to solve problems in network analysis, coding theory, and optimization. By completion, students can model complex discrete problems combinatorially and employ advanced counting techniques to derive closed-form solutions and asymptotic bounds.
126: This course examines algorithmic techniques for solving NP-hard optimization problems through polynomial-time approximation methods. Students study approximation ratios, performance guarantees, and hardness of approximation results, with emphasis on greedy algorithms, linear programming relaxations, and semidefinite programming approaches. The course covers classical problems including vertex cover, set cover, traveling salesman problem, and scheduling, analyzing both upper and lower bounds on approximation factors. Students develop skills in designing approximation algorithms, proving approximation guarantees, and understanding the limits of efficient approximation. Through problem sets and projects, students apply these techniques to real-world optimization challenges and learn to evaluate trade-offs between solution quality and computational efficiency.
127: This course examines the theoretical foundations and practical methodologies of software testing within the context of discrete mathematics and computational theory. Students study formal verification techniques, test case generation algorithms, and coverage metrics derived from graph theory and combinatorial analysis. The course covers black-box and white-box testing strategies, property-based testing frameworks, and the mathematical principles underlying test adequacy criteria. Students develop proficiency in designing comprehensive test suites, analyzing program behavior through formal specifications, and applying automated testing tools to validate correctness of algorithms and discrete structures. Upon completion, students can construct rigorous test plans for complex software systems and apply theoretical testing principles to verify implementations of discrete mathematical algorithms.

Students present and critically analyze recent publications, research papers, and ongoing projects in areas such as computational complexity, graph theory, combinatorial optimization, and formal language theory. Through peer discussion and faculty guidance, participants develop skills in research communication, technical writing, and scholarly critique while building familiarity with current methodologies and open problems in the field. The seminar cultivates the ability to identify research gaps, propose novel approaches, and contribute original insights to theoretical computer science and discrete mathematics.

142: This course covers fundamental and advanced techniques in combinatorial optimization, focusing on algorithmic approaches to solving discrete optimization problems with applications in operations research and computational mathematics. Students study classical problems including the traveling salesman problem, maximum flow, matching, and scheduling, alongside exact methods such as branch-and-bound, cutting planes, and dynamic programming. The course emphasizes both theoretical complexity analysis and practical implementation, with students developing proficiency in formulating real-world problems as integer linear programs and applying modern optimization solvers. Through computational projects, students gain hands-on experience with optimization software and learn to evaluate algorithm performance on large-scale instances. Upon completion, students can model complex discrete systems, select appropriate solution strategies, and implement efficient algorithms for combinatorial problems arising in engineering and scientific applications.
143: This course examines the formal mathematical foundations underlying programming language design and behavior. Students study denotational, operational, and axiomatic semantics frameworks, learning to formally specify language constructs and prove program properties using these approaches. The course covers lambda calculus, type systems, and formal verification techniques, with practical applications to language implementation and compiler design. Students develop the ability to analyze program correctness, reason about language features formally, and apply semantic methods to solve real-world computational problems in mathematical modeling contexts.
144: This course provides a comprehensive treatment of matrix theory and its applications to numerical computation and mathematical modeling. Students study advanced topics including matrix decompositions (QR, SVD, eigenvalue decompositions), matrix norms, conditioning and stability analysis, and iterative methods for solving linear systems. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and computational implementation, with practical work using numerical software to solve large-scale problems arising in scientific computing. Upon completion, students are able to analyze the numerical properties of matrix algorithms, select appropriate decomposition methods for specific problems, and implement efficient solutions for systems encountered in mathematical modeling applications.
145: This course covers fundamental and advanced computational algorithms for solving linear algebra problems arising in scientific computing and mathematical modeling. Students study direct and iterative methods for solving linear systems, eigenvalue computations, matrix factorizations (LU, QR, SVD), and numerical stability analysis. The course emphasizes implementation of these algorithms using modern programming languages and numerical libraries, with applications to large-scale problems in engineering and physics. Students develop proficiency in analyzing algorithmic complexity, convergence rates, and error propagation in finite precision arithmetic. By course completion, students can select appropriate algorithms for specific linear algebra problems, implement efficient solutions, and evaluate computational performance and accuracy.
146: This course provides rigorous mathematical foundations for machine learning, covering linear algebra, probability theory, and optimization techniques essential for understanding modern ML algorithms. Students study convex optimization, gradient descent methods, statistical learning theory, and regularization techniques through formal mathematical analysis. The course examines supervised and unsupervised learning models including linear regression, logistic regression, support vector machines, and neural networks from a theoretical perspective. Students develop proficiency in mathematical proofs, algorithm analysis, and implementing optimization algorithms in Python or similar computational environments. Upon completion, students can derive learning algorithms from first principles, analyze convergence properties, and apply mathematical rigor to evaluate machine learning model performance and generalization bounds.
147: This course covers theoretical foundations and practical applications of interpolation methods in multiple dimensions. Students study polynomial interpolation, radial basis functions, spline interpolation, and scattered data approximation techniques essential for multidimensional problems. The course emphasizes error analysis, convergence properties, and computational efficiency of various interpolation schemes. Students implement interpolation algorithms using MATLAB or Python and apply them to real-world problems in scientific computing, such as surface reconstruction and function approximation. Upon completion, students can select appropriate interpolation methods for multidimensional datasets, analyze their accuracy and stability, and develop efficient computational solutions for complex approximation problems.
148: This course covers advanced optimization techniques for solving complex computational problems in scientific and engineering applications. Students study both deterministic and stochastic optimization algorithms, including gradient-based methods, evolutionary algorithms, and metaheuristic approaches, with emphasis on convergence analysis and computational complexity. The course provides hands-on experience implementing optimization solvers using Python and specialized libraries such as SciPy and CVXPY, and applying these tools to constrained and unconstrained optimization problems. Students develop proficiency in formulating real-world problems as optimization models, selecting appropriate algorithms based on problem structure, and analyzing solution quality and computational efficiency. By course completion, students can design and implement optimization strategies for large-scale numerical problems arising in mathematical modeling and scientific computing.
149: This course covers fundamental and advanced machine learning algorithms within the context of numerical analysis and mathematical modeling. Students study supervised learning methods including regression, classification, and ensemble techniques, alongside unsupervised learning approaches such as clustering and dimensionality reduction. The course emphasizes the mathematical foundations of machine learning, including optimization theory, statistical learning theory, and convergence analysis of algorithms. Students gain practical experience implementing algorithms in Python using scikit-learn, TensorFlow, and other computational libraries, and apply these techniques to solve real-world modeling problems. Upon completion, students can develop, evaluate, and deploy machine learning models for predictive analysis and pattern recognition in scientific and engineering applications.
150: This course examines the theory and applications of equidistribution in sequences, focusing on how sequences of real numbers become uniformly distributed modulo one. Students study classical results including Weyl's equidistribution criterion, Kronecker's theorem, and van der Corput's difference theorem, along with modern extensions to multidimensional sequences. The course develops computational methods for analyzing distribution properties and applies equidistribution theory to quasi-Monte Carlo methods, numerical integration, and pseudorandom number generation. Students implement algorithms to test equidistribution properties and apply these techniques to solve practical problems in scientific computing and mathematical modeling.
151: This course provides advanced treatment of functional analysis concepts with direct applications to numerical methods and mathematical modeling. Students study Banach and Hilbert spaces, linear operators, spectral theory, and weak convergence, with emphasis on their role in solving differential equations and optimization problems. The course covers variational formulations, weak solutions, and Sobolev spaces essential for finite element methods and numerical approximations. Students develop proficiency in applying functional analysis frameworks to analyze convergence, stability, and error estimates in computational algorithms. Through theoretical foundations and practical applications, students gain the ability to rigorously justify numerical schemes and construct well-posed mathematical models for complex physical phenomena.
152: This course examines the theoretical foundations and practical applications of Euclidean algorithms within the context of public accounting systems and computational number theory. Students study the mathematical principles underlying greatest common divisor (GCD) computations, extended Euclidean algorithms, and their implementation in financial data processing and cryptographic verification systems. The course covers algorithm complexity analysis, modular arithmetic applications in accounting reconciliation, and the development of efficient computational methods for large-scale numerical problems. Students implement these algorithms using modern programming languages and apply them to real-world accounting scenarios involving data validation, error detection, and secure transaction verification. Upon completion, students can design and optimize Euclidean-based algorithms for specialized accounting applications and analyze their computational efficiency in practical financial systems.
153: This course covers the mathematical foundations and computational methods essential for quantitative finance and derivative pricing. Students study stochastic calculus, Itô's lemma, and partial differential equations governing financial instruments, with emphasis on the Black-Scholes model and its extensions. The course develops practical skills in implementing numerical schemes for option pricing, Monte Carlo simulations, and calibration of financial models using programming tools such as Python or MATLAB. Students apply these techniques to real market data, learning to construct and validate mathematical models for equity, fixed income, and derivative markets. Upon completion, students are equipped to develop pricing algorithms, perform risk analysis, and solve complex financial engineering problems in both academic and industry settings.
154: This course covers the mathematical foundations and computational theory of spline functions, including polynomial splines, B-splines, and rational splines. Students develop proficiency in constructing and analyzing spline interpolation and approximation methods, with emphasis on smoothness conditions, knot placement strategies, and convergence properties. The course addresses practical applications in curve and surface fitting, numerical differentiation and integration, and the solution of differential equations using spline-based methods. Students implement spline algorithms in computational environments and apply them to real-world modeling problems in engineering and scientific computing. Upon completion, students can design optimal spline representations for complex data sets and evaluate their numerical stability and approximation accuracy.
155: This course covers fundamental algorithms and computational techniques for solving discrete geometric problems in two and three dimensions. Students study convex hulls, Voronoi diagrams, Delaunay triangulations, and polygon clipping algorithms, implementing these structures using C++ or Python. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical applications, including computational complexity analysis and numerical stability considerations. Students develop robust geometric software libraries and apply them to real-world problems in computational physics, computer graphics, and optimization. By course completion, students can design and implement efficient geometric algorithms, analyze their performance characteristics, and apply them to complex mathematical modeling scenarios.
156: This course covers the fundamental theory and practical applications of digital signal processing (DSP) within the context of mathematical modelling. Students study discrete-time signals and systems, z-transforms, discrete Fourier transforms (DFT), and fast Fourier transform (FFT) algorithms for efficient signal analysis. The course emphasizes filter design techniques, including FIR and IIR filter implementation, and spectral analysis methods for extracting meaningful information from noisy data. Students develop proficiency with DSP software tools and programming environments to implement algorithms, analyze real-world signals, and solve problems in signal reconstruction, noise reduction, and feature extraction. Upon completion, students can design and implement digital filters, perform frequency-domain analysis of complex signals, and apply DSP techniques to mathematical modelling problems in engineering and scientific applications.
157: This course examines the mathematical frameworks and computational techniques for modeling complex biophysical phenomena, including protein dynamics, cellular signaling, and biomolecular interactions. Students develop proficiency in formulating differential equations, stochastic models, and multiscale simulation approaches to represent biological processes at molecular and cellular scales. The course covers numerical methods for solving nonlinear systems, parameter estimation techniques, and validation strategies using experimental data. Students apply computational tools such as MATLAB and specialized biophysics software to implement and analyze models of enzyme kinetics, membrane transport, and gene regulatory networks. Upon completion, students can construct predictive biophysical models, interpret simulation results critically, and communicate findings through scientific visualization and technical documentation.

Through theoretical analysis and computational exercises, students develop the ability to implement graphics algorithms, analyze their numerical stability, and design efficient mathematical models for 3D visualization and animation systems.
159: This course examines theoretical foundations and practical applications of regularization techniques for solving ill-posed problems in numerical analysis and mathematical modeling. Through computational projects, students implement regularization algorithms in MATLAB or Python and analyze their performance on benchmark problems. Upon completion, students can identify ill-posed problems, select appropriate regularization methods, and develop robust numerical solutions for applications in engineering and scientific computing.

242: This course covers fundamental numerical techniques for solving linear algebra problems that arise in scientific computing and engineering applications. Students learn direct methods (Gaussian elimination, LU decomposition, QR factorization) and iterative methods (Jacobi, Gauss-Seidel, conjugate gradient) for solving systems of linear equations, along with algorithms for eigenvalue computation and matrix decomposition. The course emphasizes computational stability, error analysis, and algorithmic complexity, with practical implementation using programming languages and numerical libraries. Students develop proficiency in selecting appropriate methods based on matrix properties (sparsity, conditioning, symmetry) and implementing efficient solutions for large-scale problems. Upon completion, students can analyze numerical stability of algorithms, implement standard linear algebra solvers, and apply these techniques to real-world computational problems in physics, engineering, and data science.
243: This course covers the theory and applications of complex-valued functions, including complex differentiation, analytic functions, and the Cauchy-Riemann equations. Students study contour integration, residue theory, and conformal mappings, developing the ability to evaluate complex integrals and solve boundary value problems. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical computational techniques, enabling students to apply complex analysis methods to problems in physics, engineering, and applied mathematics. Through problem sets and examinations, students demonstrate proficiency in manipulating complex functions and applying residue calculus to real-world applications.
244: This course covers fundamental data structures essential for efficient algorithm design and software development. Students learn to implement and analyze arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs, and hash tables, understanding their time and space complexity characteristics. The course emphasizes practical programming skills using languages such as C++ or Python, enabling students to select appropriate data structures for specific computational problems. Through problem-solving exercises and projects, students develop the ability to design algorithms that optimize memory usage and execution time. Upon completion, students can construct complex data structures, evaluate their performance trade-offs, and apply them to real-world applications in software engineering and computational problem-solving.
245: This course introduces students to fundamental machine learning concepts, algorithms, and applications within the context of data-driven problem solving. Students learn supervised learning techniques including linear regression, logistic regression, decision trees, and support vector machines, alongside unsupervised methods such as clustering and dimensionality reduction. The course covers essential tools and libraries including Python, scikit-learn, and pandas for implementing machine learning models on real-world datasets. Students develop practical skills in data preprocessing, feature engineering, model evaluation, and hyperparameter tuning to build effective predictive systems. By course completion, students are able to select appropriate algorithms for specific problems, train and validate models, and interpret results to make data-informed decisions.
246: This course covers the foundational principles of mathematical logic, including propositional logic, predicate logic, and formal systems of reasoning. Students study truth tables, logical equivalences, quantifiers, and methods of proof such as natural deduction and resolution. The course examines the completeness and soundness of logical systems, as well as fundamental concepts like consistency, validity, and satisfiability. Through problem-solving and formal derivations, students develop the ability to construct rigorous mathematical proofs and analyze the logical structure of mathematical arguments. This course provides essential preparation for advanced topics in computability theory, automated reasoning, and formal verification.
247: Mathematical Analysis-1 introduces students to the foundational concepts of real analysis and single-variable calculus. The course covers limits, continuity, differentiation, and integration of real functions, with rigorous proofs of fundamental theorems including the Intermediate Value Theorem and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Students develop proficiency in computing derivatives and integrals, analyzing function behavior, and applying calculus techniques to optimization and rate-of-change problems. Upon completion, students are able to construct rigorous mathematical arguments, solve complex analysis problems, and apply analytical methods to model real-world phenomena in computer science and applied mathematics.
248: This course covers advanced topics in mathematical analysis including sequences and series of functions, uniform convergence, power series, and Fourier series. Students develop rigorous understanding of multivariable calculus, partial derivatives, multiple integrals, and vector calculus through formal proofs and theoretical foundations. The course emphasizes applications of these concepts to optimization problems, differential equations, and physical phenomena. Upon completion, students are able to analyze convergence properties of function sequences, compute and manipulate power and Fourier series expansions, solve multivariable optimization problems, and apply vector calculus to real-world applications in physics and engineering.
249: This course covers fundamental and advanced concepts in graph theory, including graph representations, connectivity, paths, cycles, and tree structures. Students learn to analyze graph properties using adjacency matrices, adjacency lists, and incidence matrices, and apply classical algorithms such as depth-first search, breadth-first search, and shortest path computations. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations—including planarity, colorability, and matching theory—and practical problem-solving through implementation of graph algorithms in programming languages. By course completion, students can model real-world problems as graphs, select appropriate algorithms for specific applications, and implement efficient solutions for network analysis, optimization, and combinatorial problems.
250: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles and architecture of computer networks. Students study the OSI and TCP/IP reference models, network protocols, IP addressing, routing algorithms, and data link layer technologies including Ethernet and wireless standards. The course covers practical networking concepts such as DNS, DHCP, NAT, and basic network security principles. Through hands-on exercises, students configure network devices, analyze network traffic using packet analysis tools, and troubleshoot common connectivity issues. Upon completion, students can design simple network topologies, understand how data is transmitted across networks, and apply foundational knowledge to more advanced networking courses.
251: This course covers the foundational concepts of single-variable calculus essential for applied mathematics and computer science. Students study limits, continuity, derivatives, and their applications to optimization, curve sketching, and rate-of-change problems. The course develops proficiency in computing derivatives using differentiation rules, the chain rule, and implicit differentiation, with emphasis on practical problem-solving in engineering and scientific contexts. Through rigorous mathematical reasoning and computational practice, students gain the analytical tools necessary for advanced mathematics courses and quantitative applications in informatics.
252: Mathematical Analysis - 3 continues the rigorous study of real analysis, focusing on multivariable calculus and advanced topics in differential and integral calculus. Students examine partial derivatives, multiple integrals, vector calculus, and applications of these concepts to optimization problems and differential equations. The course develops proficiency in computing limits, derivatives, and integrals in higher dimensions, as well as applying theorems such as Green's, Stokes', and the divergence theorem. Upon completion, students are able to analyze functions of several variables, solve complex optimization problems, and apply calculus techniques to problems in physics and engineering relevant to informatics applications.
253: This course covers advanced topics in discrete mathematics essential for computer science and applied mathematics. Students study graph theory, including trees, connectivity, and algorithms for shortest paths and minimum spanning trees; combinatorics with emphasis on permutations, combinations, and recurrence relations; and Boolean algebra with applications to logic circuits and digital systems. The course develops problem-solving skills through rigorous proofs and computational techniques, enabling students to analyze algorithmic complexity and design efficient solutions to discrete optimization problems. Practical applications include network analysis, cryptography fundamentals, and coding theory relevant to modern computing systems.
254: Programming - 2 builds on foundational programming concepts by introducing object-oriented programming (OOP) principles, data structures, and algorithmic problem-solving. Students learn to design and implement programs using classes, inheritance, polymorphism, and encapsulation while working with fundamental data structures such as arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, and trees. The course emphasizes writing efficient, maintainable code through hands-on projects in languages such as C++ or Java, with practical applications in real-world software development scenarios. Students develop the ability to analyze algorithmic complexity, select appropriate data structures for specific problems, and debug complex programs systematically. By course completion, students can architect moderately complex applications, implement standard algorithms, and apply OOP design patterns to solve computational problems effectively.
255: This course covers the fundamental principles and practical techniques of web application development using modern programming languages and frameworks. Students learn front-end technologies including HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, alongside back-end development with server-side languages such as Python or PHP, and database design with SQL. The course emphasizes full-stack development, teaching students to build dynamic, responsive web applications that integrate client-side interfaces with server-side logic and data persistence. Through hands-on projects, students develop proficiency in version control systems, debugging tools, and deployment practices, enabling them to design and implement complete web solutions from conception to production.
256: Mathematical Analysis - 2 continues the study of real analysis, focusing on multivariable calculus and infinite series. Students explore partial derivatives, multiple integrals, vector calculus, and convergence of sequences and series of functions. The course develops rigorous proofs of fundamental theorems including the implicit function theorem, Fubini's theorem, and Stokes' theorem. Through problem sets and applications, students master techniques for analyzing functions of several variables and applying calculus to optimization and physical systems. Upon completion, students can solve complex problems involving multivariable functions, evaluate integrals in multiple dimensions, and apply analytical methods to applied mathematics and computational problems.
257: This course introduces fundamental programming concepts and practices using a modern programming language. Students learn core programming constructs including variables, data types, control flow, functions, and basic data structures such as arrays and strings. The course emphasizes problem-solving methodology and algorithmic thinking through hands-on coding exercises and projects. By the end of the course, students are able to write, debug, and test simple programs to solve computational problems and understand the foundational principles necessary for advanced programming courses.
258: This course covers fundamental mathematical concepts and analytical geometry essential for applied mathematics and computer science. Students study vector algebra, coordinate systems, conic sections, and three-dimensional geometry, developing proficiency in geometric transformations and spatial visualization. The course emphasizes analytical methods for solving geometric problems using algebraic techniques and coordinate-based approaches. Upon completion, students can apply geometric principles to computational problems, model spatial relationships mathematically, and utilize analytical geometry in algorithm design and data visualization applications.
259: This course introduces students to fundamental concepts in discrete mathematics essential for computer science and applied mathematics. Students study set theory, logic, combinatorics, graph theory basics, and mathematical proofs, developing rigorous reasoning skills required for algorithm design and analysis. The course emphasizes problem-solving techniques including counting principles, permutations, combinations, and logical argumentation through direct proof, proof by contradiction, and mathematical induction. Students learn to model real-world problems using discrete structures and apply these models to solve computational challenges. Upon completion, students can construct formal proofs, analyze combinatorial problems, and apply graph-theoretic concepts to practical applications in computer science.
260: This course introduces students to graphical user interface (GUI) design and development using modern frameworks and programming languages. Students learn fundamental GUI concepts including event-driven programming, layout management, widget hierarchies, and user interaction patterns through hands-on projects. The course covers industry-standard tools and libraries such as Qt, JavaFX, or Tkinter, enabling students to build responsive desktop applications with professional-quality interfaces. Students develop practical skills in designing intuitive user experiences, implementing event handlers, managing application state, and debugging GUI-based programs. By course completion, students can design and implement functional GUI applications that effectively integrate backend logic with user-friendly frontend components.
261: This course examines the theoretical foundations of translation as both a linguistic and cultural practice, with emphasis on formal models and computational approaches. Students study major translation theories including equivalence-based, functionalist, and descriptive approaches, analyzing how meaning transfers across language pairs and cultural contexts. The course covers practical applications of translation theory to machine translation systems, localization processes, and multilingual natural language processing. Through case studies and analysis of translated texts, students develop critical frameworks for evaluating translation quality and identifying systematic patterns in translation choices. Upon completion, students will be able to apply theoretical principles to assess translations, design translation workflows, and understand the linguistic constraints that inform both human and automated translation systems.
262: This course introduces students to the mathematical foundations and computational techniques of digital signal and data analysis. Students learn discrete mathematics concepts, Fourier analysis, wavelet transforms, and statistical methods for processing digital signals and datasets. The course covers practical implementation using programming languages and specialized software tools for signal filtering, feature extraction, and pattern recognition. Upon completion, students are able to apply digital analysis techniques to real-world problems in engineering, data science, and scientific computing, and can design and implement algorithms for processing discrete data in various application domains.
263: This course examines the mathematical frameworks and analytical techniques essential for modeling and solving problems in natural sciences. Students study differential equations, partial differential equations, vector calculus, and linear algebra as applied to physics, chemistry, and biology. The course develops proficiency in mathematical modeling, numerical methods, and computational tools for simulating natural phenomena. Students learn to formulate scientific problems mathematically, select appropriate solution methods, and interpret results within their physical context. Upon completion, students can apply advanced mathematical techniques to analyze experimental data and construct predictive models in their respective scientific disciplines.
264: This course covers fundamental data structures essential for efficient algorithm design and software development. Students learn to implement and analyze arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs, and hash tables, understanding their performance characteristics through Big O notation. The course emphasizes practical problem-solving using C++ or Python, requiring students to select appropriate data structures for specific computational tasks and optimize code for time and space complexity. By course completion, students can design scalable solutions to complex problems, implement custom data structures, and evaluate trade-offs between different structural approaches in real-world applications.
265: This course examines the fundamental principles of computer architecture, including processor design, memory hierarchies, instruction sets, and the von Neumann model. Students learn assembly language programming for x86/x64 processors, gaining hands-on experience writing low-level code that directly manipulates hardware resources, manages memory, and handles interrupts. The course covers digital logic fundamentals, CPU execution cycles, cache optimization, and system-level programming concepts essential for understanding how high-level code translates to machine operations. Through practical assignments, students develop proficiency in debugging assembly code, optimizing performance at the hardware level, and interfacing with operating system services. Upon completion, students can write efficient assembly programs, analyze processor behavior, and apply architectural knowledge to optimize software performance.
266: This course provides students with a rigorous foundation in functional analysis, covering vector spaces, normed spaces, Banach spaces, and Hilbert spaces. Students study linear operators, bounded operators, and spectral theory, developing proficiency in analyzing infinite-dimensional spaces and their properties. The course emphasizes applications to differential equations, optimization problems, and computational mathematics relevant to applied informatics. Through theoretical proofs and problem-solving, students learn to apply functional analysis techniques to solve complex mathematical problems arising in engineering and scientific computing. Upon completion, students can analyze functional spaces, work with operator theory, and apply these concepts to real-world applications in applied mathematics and computer science.
267: This course examines the qualitative behavior of solutions to differential equations without requiring explicit analytical solutions. Students study phase plane analysis, stability theory, and bifurcation phenomena to understand long-term dynamics of nonlinear systems. The course covers equilibrium points, limit cycles, Lyapunov functions, and perturbation methods, with applications to physical and biological systems. Students develop proficiency in constructing phase portraits, analyzing stability using eigenvalue methods, and predicting system behavior under parameter variations. Upon completion, students can classify dynamical systems, determine stability of equilibria, and apply qualitative techniques to model real-world phenomena in engineering and natural sciences.
268: This course covers fundamental and advanced combinatorial algorithms essential for solving discrete optimization problems. Students study graph algorithms, including traversal, shortest path, and network flow techniques, alongside combinatorial optimization methods such as dynamic programming, greedy algorithms, and backtracking. The course emphasizes algorithmic complexity analysis and practical implementation using programming languages like C++ or Python. Students develop proficiency in designing efficient solutions for NP-hard problems and analyzing trade-offs between solution quality and computational resources. By course completion, students can select appropriate algorithmic approaches for real-world combinatorial problems and implement optimized solutions with rigorous complexity justification.
269: This course covers fundamental and advanced algorithms for solving problems on graph structures, including traversal methods (breadth-first and depth-first search), shortest path algorithms (Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall), and minimum spanning tree construction (Kruskal, Prim). Students develop proficiency in analyzing algorithm complexity, implementing solutions in standard programming languages, and selecting appropriate algorithms for specific graph problems. The course emphasizes both theoretical understanding of graph theory concepts and practical application to real-world problems such as network optimization, routing, and connectivity analysis. Upon completion, students are able to design efficient graph-based solutions, implement algorithms correctly, and evaluate their performance characteristics.
270: Students engage in supervised practical work within industry or research organizations, applying theoretical knowledge from their informatics and applied mathematics coursework to real-world problems. The course develops professional competencies in software development, data analysis, algorithm implementation, and mathematical modeling through hands-on project work under mentor guidance. Participants gain experience with industry-standard tools, version control systems, and collaborative development practices while working on substantive technical problems. Upon completion, students demonstrate the ability to translate academic concepts into functional solutions, document technical work professionally, and integrate into professional computing environments. This practical experience bridges academic study and career preparation, providing portfolio-building opportunities and professional networking within the informatics sector.
271: This course introduces students to the mathematical foundations of cybernetics and information theory, emphasizing control systems, feedback mechanisms, and information processing. Students study automata theory, Boolean functions, and computational models to understand how systems self-regulate and process information. The course covers formal methods for analyzing system behavior, stability conditions, and decision-making algorithms. Through problem-solving and theoretical analysis, students develop the ability to model complex systems mathematically and apply cybernetic principles to real-world control and communication problems. The course prepares students for advanced work in systems theory, artificial intelligence, and computational mathematics.
272: This course examines advanced methodologies and theoretical frameworks in action research, emphasizing systematic inquiry into professional practice and organizational problems. Students develop competencies in designing action research projects, collecting and analyzing qualitative and quantitative data, and implementing iterative cycles of planning, action, observation, and reflection. The course covers research design documentation, ethical considerations in participatory research, and strategies for translating findings into evidence-based improvements. Students apply these methods to real-world informatics and applied mathematics contexts, producing a comprehensive action research proposal or case study that demonstrates their ability to bridge theory and practice in their professional domain.
273: This course develops students' proficiency in modern Armenian language and effective communication skills within academic and professional contexts. Students study grammatical structures, vocabulary expansion, and stylistic conventions essential for technical writing and formal discourse in information security fields. The course emphasizes oral presentation techniques, argumentation, and written composition to enable students to articulate complex security concepts clearly to diverse audiences. Through analysis of authentic texts and guided practice, students cultivate the ability to communicate security findings, policy recommendations, and technical documentation with precision and cultural appropriateness. By course completion, students demonstrate competency in constructing well-structured arguments and producing professional-level Armenian language communications required in cybersecurity practice.
274: This course examines fundamental philosophical concepts and methodologies essential for developing critical thinking in information security contexts. Students engage with epistemology, logic, and ethics to understand knowledge validation, reasoning structures, and moral frameworks governing cybersecurity practices. The course explores philosophical foundations of privacy, autonomy, and responsibility as they apply to digital systems and data protection. Through analysis of classical and contemporary philosophical texts, students develop analytical skills necessary for evaluating security policies, assessing ethical dilemmas in information systems, and constructing reasoned arguments in professional security discourse. Students will be able to apply philosophical reasoning to complex security challenges and articulate principled positions on emerging information security issues.
275: This course examines the principles of ecology and environmental systems relevant to information security infrastructure and sustainable technology practices. Students study ecosystem dynamics, biodiversity, pollution mechanisms, and climate change impacts while exploring the environmental footprint of data centers, computing systems, and electronic waste management. The course covers environmental protection regulations, green computing standards, and lifecycle assessment methodologies for IT equipment. Students develop competency in evaluating environmental risks associated with information technology operations and implementing sustainable practices within security-focused organizations. Upon completion, students can assess environmental compliance requirements for IT infrastructure and contribute to corporate sustainability initiatives in the information security sector.
276: This course develops advanced Russian language proficiency for information security students, building upon foundational skills with emphasis on technical and professional communication. Students engage with specialized vocabulary related to cybersecurity, network protocols, and information systems through authentic Russian texts, academic articles, and professional documentation. The course covers complex grammatical structures, including conditional constructions and advanced syntax, enabling students to comprehend and produce sophisticated written and oral discourse. Students practice technical translation, report writing, and professional correspondence relevant to the information security field, preparing them for international collaboration and documentation review in Russian-speaking contexts. By course completion, students demonstrate intermediate-advanced proficiency in reading, writing, and speaking Russian within professional and academic settings.
277: This course examines the political, social, and cultural developments of Armenia from the medieval period through the modern era, with emphasis on key transformations during the Ottoman, Persian, and Russian imperial periods. Students analyze primary historical documents, archaeological evidence, and scholarly interpretations to understand Armenia's complex geopolitical position and its impact on national identity formation. The course covers critical events including the Armenian Genocide of 1915, the Soviet period, and Armenia's independence and contemporary challenges. Through comparative historical analysis, students develop critical thinking skills applicable to understanding how historical context shapes contemporary security and geopolitical issues. This foundational knowledge supports information security professionals in understanding the cultural and historical dimensions of their work within Armenian institutions and society.
278: This course examines the political, social, and cultural development of Armenia from ancient times through the medieval period. Students analyze primary historical sources and archaeological evidence to understand the formation of Armenian identity, the establishment of Christianity as the state religion in 301 CE, and Armenia's interactions with neighboring empires. The course develops critical thinking and research skills essential for understanding how historical context shapes contemporary geopolitical and security issues. Students will be able to contextualize Armenia's historical significance within broader regional and global frameworks relevant to information security studies.
279: This course equips students with essential knowledge and practical skills for responding to emergency situations and protecting civilian populations during crises. Through hands-on training and simulations, students develop competency in emergency communication, evacuation procedures, and coordination with emergency services. Upon completion, students are prepared to contribute effectively to organizational emergency response teams and understand the intersection of physical and cybersecurity in crisis management.

Through structured exercises in reading, writing, listening, and speaking, students gain the ability to comprehend Russian technical documentation, participate in professional discussions, and communicate effectively in multilingual security environments. The course prepares students for advanced Russian language study and facilitates access to Russian-language cybersecurity resources and international collaboration within the post-Soviet technology sector.
281: This course develops advanced proficiency in Armenian language and professional communication skills essential for information security specialists. The course covers rhetoric, argumentation, and presentation techniques tailored to cybersecurity contexts, enabling students to communicate complex technical concepts clearly to both technical and non-technical audiences. Through practical exercises, students enhance their ability to analyze and produce high-quality Armenian texts in professional settings, strengthening their capacity to function effectively in Armenian-language work environments within the information security field.

292: This course examines the philosophical and practical foundations of ethics as they apply to information security and technology professionals. 293: This course examines fundamental principles and contemporary developments in natural science disciplines relevant to information security professionals. Through theoretical study and practical examples, students develop scientific literacy necessary to understand emerging security technologies and evaluate their physical feasibility and limitations. This interdisciplinary foundation enables information security specialists to comprehend the scientific basis of advanced cryptographic methods and next-generation security systems.
294: This course introduces information security students to core business principles and organizational structures relevant to cybersecurity governance and risk management. 295: This course examines the legal frameworks governing information security, cybercrime, and data protection within national and international contexts. Through case analysis and statutory interpretation, students develop the ability to identify legal risks, assess regulatory compliance obligations, and advise on lawful security practices in organizational settings.
296: This course covers statistical methods and techniques essential for information security analysis and risk assessment. Upon completion, students can apply statistical reasoning to identify vulnerabilities, assess threat probabilities, and make data-driven security decisions.
297: This course examines the historical development, core doctrines, and social structures of major world religions including Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Buddhism, and Hinduism. 298: This course develops professional communication competencies essential for information security practitioners in technical and organizational contexts. Students practice drafting security assessments, creating executive summaries, and delivering technical briefings while maintaining clarity and precision. Upon completion, students will effectively communicate security findings, recommendations, and risk analyses in formats appropriate for their intended audience.
299: This course examines core psychological principles and human behavior patterns relevant to information security contexts. Students explore cognitive biases, decision-making processes, and social engineering vulnerabilities to understand how psychological factors influence security breaches and user compliance. Through case studies and practical scenarios, students develop the ability to design security awareness programs, anticipate human vulnerabilities in security systems, and implement user-centered security policies that account for psychological realities rather than assuming purely rational behavior.
300: This course develops advanced English language proficiency for information security professionals, emphasizing technical communication and specialized vocabulary in cybersecurity contexts. 301: This course examines the theoretical foundations and methodological approaches to understanding culture as a complex social phenomenon. The course analyzes how cultural artifacts, institutions, and practices reflect and shape social structures, with particular attention to the intersection of culture and information systems. Through critical analysis of case studies and primary sources, students develop skills in cultural interpretation and contextual analysis applicable to security and information governance contexts. 302: This course develops advanced Russian language proficiency for information security professionals, building upon intermediate competencies in reading, writing, listening, and speaking. 303: This course examines the foundational concepts and theories of sociology as they relate to social structures, institutions, and human behavior within information security contexts. 564: This course covers fundamental and advanced techniques in signal processing with applications to physics and artificial intelligence. 565: This course covers the fundamental principles of thermodynamics and statistical mechanics, bridging macroscopic thermodynamic phenomena with microscopic molecular behavior. Through problem sets and computational exercises, students learn to model thermal systems, analyze equilibrium states, and apply statistical reasoning to data analysis and AI algorithms. 569: Machine Learning-2 builds on foundational concepts to cover advanced supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms, including support vector machines, ensemble methods, neural networks, and clustering techniques. 572: This course provides students with foundational knowledge in probability theory and statistical methods essential for data analysis in physics and machine learning applications. Through problem sets and computational exercises, students develop proficiency in statistical software and learn to apply these concepts to real datasets from physics experiments and AI training scenarios. 573: Mathematical Analysis-1 provides foundational concepts in differential and integral calculus essential for advanced physics and machine learning applications. Through problem-solving and theoretical exercises, students gain proficiency in analyzing function behavior and applying calculus to real-world data processing scenarios. 574: This course covers the theory and applications of ordinary and partial differential equations essential for modeling physical systems and machine learning algorithms. 575: This course develops advanced mathematical foundations essential for data processing and artificial intelligence applications in physics. 576: This course covers the theory and applications of complex functions, including analytic functions, Cauchy-Riemann equations, and contour integration. 578: This course introduces students to the fundamental concepts and algorithms of machine learning within the context of physics applications and data analysis. 585: This course examines the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of telecommunication systems through computational modeling and simulation. 589: This course examines the mathematical foundations and practical principles underlying digital signal and data processing systems.
