590: This course teaches students to develop computational models for complex radiophysical phenomena using numerical methods and simulation techniques. Through hands-on projects, students gain proficiency in scientific computing libraries, data visualization tools, and high-performance computing practices. 591: This course covers the fundamental theory and practical applications of digital signal processing (DSP) in physics and artificial intelligence contexts. Students learn discrete-time signal analysis, Fourier transforms, filtering techniques, and spectral estimation methods essential for processing experimental and computational data. 592: This course provides students with comprehensive training in the theory and implementation of neural networks for physics applications and artificial intelligence. Students learn fundamental concepts including network architectures (feedforward, convolutional, and recurrent networks), backpropagation algorithms, activation functions, and optimization techniques such as stochastic gradient descent and adaptive learning rate methods. The course covers practical implementation using Python-based frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch, with emphasis on building, training, and validating models for regression, classification, and pattern recognition tasks. 593: This course covers fundamental and advanced optimization techniques essential for solving complex problems in physics and machine learning. Students study linear programming, convex optimization, gradient descent methods, and stochastic optimization algorithms, with emphasis on both theoretical foundations and practical implementation. Students learn to formulate optimization problems, select appropriate algorithms based on problem characteristics, and analyze convergence properties and computational efficiency. 594: This course covers the fundamental principles of semiconductor devices and their applications in modern electronic circuits. 595: This course provides students with a rigorous foundation in functional analysis, emphasizing infinite-dimensional vector spaces and linear operators essential for advanced physics and machine learning applications. The course covers first aid techniques, triage procedures, and medical response in mass casualty scenarios, with emphasis on radiation safety and contamination control. Through hands-on training and simulations, students develop competency in emergency assessment, victim stabilization, and coordination with emergency services. Upon completion, students are prepared to implement protective measures, provide immediate medical assistance, and contribute to emergency management operations in their professional capacity.
620: This course examines the philosophical foundations and practical applications of ethics within scientific research and technological development. Students explore ethical frameworks, professional codes of conduct, and moral decision-making processes relevant to radiophysics and computer technology fields. The course addresses contemporary issues including data privacy, cybersecurity ethics, responsible innovation, and the societal impact of emerging technologies. Through case studies and critical analysis, students develop the ability to identify ethical dilemmas in their discipline and apply ethical reasoning to real-world technical problems. Upon completion, students are equipped to navigate ethical challenges in research, engineering practice, and technology deployment.
621: This course examines fundamental principles and recent developments across physics, chemistry, and biology that underpin modern scientific understanding. Students explore quantum mechanics, relativity, thermodynamics, atomic structure, and molecular interactions, alongside contemporary topics in genetics, ecology, and cosmology. The course emphasizes the interconnections between disciplines and demonstrates how theoretical concepts apply to technological innovations in radiophysics and computing. Through problem-solving exercises and laboratory work, students develop critical thinking skills and gain proficiency in scientific reasoning and data interpretation. Upon completion, students will articulate complex natural phenomena using appropriate scientific terminology and apply foundational knowledge to specialized coursework in their radiophysics and computer technology program.

Through case studies and practical exercises, students develop skills in business communication, decision-making, and project management applicable to radiophysics and computer technology ventures. Through case studies and practical exercises, students learn to identify legal risks in technology projects, understand licensing requirements, and navigate regulatory frameworks affecting their professional practice. Upon completion, students are equipped to work effectively with legal professionals and make informed decisions regarding legal compliance in technical and entrepreneurial endeavors.
624: This course covers fundamental and applied statistical methods essential for analyzing experimental data in radiophysics and computer technology. Students apply these techniques to real datasets from radiophysics experiments and computational systems, gaining practical experience in designing experiments, validating results, and drawing evidence-based conclusions. Upon completion, students can independently conduct statistical analyses, interpret complex datasets, and communicate findings through appropriate visualizations and reports.

626: This course develops students' professional communication competencies essential for careers in radiophysics and technology sectors. 627: This course introduces students to core psychological principles and theories essential for understanding human behavior and cognition. 628: This course develops advanced English language proficiency for radiophysics and computer technology students, emphasizing technical communication and specialized vocabulary in electronics, signal processing, and computing systems. 629: This course examines the theoretical foundations and methodological approaches of cultural studies as an interdisciplinary field. The course develops critical analytical skills for interpreting cultural artifacts, institutions, and practices through multiple theoretical frameworks drawn from anthropology, sociology, and media studies. 630: This course develops advanced Russian language proficiency for radiophysics and computer technology students, emphasizing technical vocabulary and specialized terminology relevant to their field. 631: This course introduces students to core sociological concepts, theories, and research methodologies essential for understanding social structures and human behavior. Students examine classical and contemporary sociological perspectives, including functionalism, conflict theory, and symbolic interactionism, while analyzing institutions such as family, education, economy, and politics. Students apply sociological frameworks to contemporary social issues and learn to interpret quantitative and qualitative data relevant to social research. Upon completion, students can evaluate social problems systematically and understand how sociological knowledge complements technical expertise in radiophysics and computer technology fields.
632: This course introduces students to fundamental economic principles and their applications within technological and industrial contexts. Students examine microeconomic concepts including supply and demand, market structures, pricing mechanisms, and consumer behavior, alongside macroeconomic topics such as inflation, unemployment, and economic growth. The course emphasizes how economic analysis applies to technology sectors, resource allocation in research and development, and cost-benefit analysis for engineering projects. Through problem-solving exercises and case studies, students develop skills in economic modeling, data interpretation, and decision-making relevant to technology-based enterprises. Upon completion, students can evaluate economic feasibility of technical projects, understand market dynamics affecting technology industries, and apply economic reasoning to professional and organizational contexts.
633: This course introduces students to the mathematical foundations of logic and its applications in computer science and radiophysics. Students study propositional logic, predicate logic, logical inference rules, and formal proof techniques, developing the ability to construct and validate logical arguments. The course covers truth tables, Boolean algebra, and logical equivalences, with emphasis on translating natural language statements into formal logical notation. Through problem-solving exercises, students learn to apply logical reasoning to circuit design, algorithm verification, and system specification. By course completion, students can analyze complex logical problems, design logical systems, and apply formal logic principles to engineering and computational challenges.
634: This course introduces students to core concepts and theories in political science, examining the structure and function of political systems, institutions, and processes. Students analyze different forms of government, political ideologies, and the mechanisms of state power while developing critical thinking skills applicable to understanding contemporary political issues. The course covers foundational topics including political theory, comparative politics, and international relations, providing context for how political systems operate across diverse societies. Through case studies and analytical frameworks, students gain the ability to evaluate political phenomena and understand the relationship between political institutions and technological societies. This course serves as essential background for radiophysics and computer technology professionals who engage with policy, governance, and the societal implications of technological advancement.
635: This course covers the fundamental principles of classical electrodynamics, including Maxwell's equations, electromagnetic wave propagation, and radiation phenomena. Students study electric and magnetic fields in various media, boundary conditions, and the behavior of electromagnetic waves in free space and conducting materials. The course develops mathematical skills in vector calculus and differential equations essential for solving electromagnetic problems. Students learn to analyze antenna theory, waveguides, and transmission line characteristics, applying these concepts to practical radiophysics applications. Upon completion, students can model electromagnetic phenomena, design basic radiating systems, and understand the physical foundations underlying modern wireless communication and radar technologies.
636: This course examines the fundamental principles of laser operation and their application in modern optical communication systems. Students study laser physics, including stimulated emission, population inversion, and various laser types (solid-state, gas, semiconductor, and fiber lasers), alongside optical fiber properties, signal modulation, and transmission characteristics. The course covers key components of optical communication systems such as transmitters, receivers, photodetectors, and amplifiers, with emphasis on wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) and dense WDM (DWDM) technologies. Through theoretical analysis and practical laboratory work, students develop competency in designing optical links, calculating system performance metrics, and troubleshooting signal degradation issues. Upon completion, students can analyze laser-based communication architectures and implement solutions for long-distance, high-bandwidth data transmission.
637: This course teaches students to develop computational models of physical phenomena using numerical methods and simulation techniques. Students learn to formulate physical problems mathematically, implement solutions using programming languages such as C++ or Python, and validate results against analytical solutions and experimental data. The course covers finite difference methods, ordinary and partial differential equations solvers, and visualization of simulation results. Students apply these skills to model systems across mechanics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics, and quantum mechanics, gaining practical experience with scientific computing libraries and high-performance computing concepts. Upon completion, students can design, implement, and analyze computer simulations of complex physical systems relevant to radiophysics applications.
638: This course introduces students to the principles and practices of electronic circuit design, covering fundamental concepts in circuit theory, component selection, and practical implementation. Students learn to analyze and design circuits using Kirchhoff's laws, Thevenin and Norton equivalents, and frequency response analysis, while gaining proficiency with circuit simulation tools such as SPICE and schematic capture software. The course emphasizes both passive and active circuit elements, including resistors, capacitors, inductors, operational amplifiers, and transistors, with applications to signal conditioning and amplification. Through laboratory work and design projects, students develop the ability to prototype circuits, troubleshoot hardware, and validate designs against specifications. Upon completion, students are prepared to apply circuit design principles to radiophysics applications and embedded systems development.
639: This course covers the mathematical foundations of information theory and the principles of error-correcting codes essential for reliable data transmission and storage. Students study Shannon's entropy, channel capacity, source coding, and the theoretical limits of information compression and transmission. The course examines fundamental coding schemes including Hamming codes, cyclic codes, convolutional codes, and turbo codes, with emphasis on encoding and decoding algorithms. Through practical exercises, students develop skills in analyzing code performance, calculating information-theoretic bounds, and implementing coding systems for communication channels. Upon completion, students can design and evaluate coding schemes for specific communication applications and understand the trade-offs between code complexity, error correction capability, and transmission efficiency.
640: This course provides students with a comprehensive foundation in probability theory and its applications to radiophysical systems and signal processing. Students study fundamental concepts including probability distributions, random processes, stochastic differential equations, and statistical inference methods essential for analyzing noisy electromagnetic signals and communication systems. The course covers both discrete and continuous probability models, with emphasis on Gaussian processes, spectral analysis, and correlation functions commonly encountered in radio wave propagation and antenna theory. Through theoretical lectures and computational exercises, students develop skills in statistical hypothesis testing, parameter estimation, and Monte Carlo simulation techniques using mathematical software. Upon completion, students are able to model and analyze random phenomena in radiophysical experiments, design optimal receivers for noisy signals, and apply statistical methods to validate experimental data in electromagnetic and communication applications.
641: This course covers advanced topics in radio engineering and stochastic processes essential for radiophysics applications. Students study noise theory, random signal analysis, spectral characteristics of fluctuations, and their effects on radio communication systems. The course develops competency in mathematical modeling of noise phenomena, signal detection in noisy environments, and optimization of receiver circuits. Through theoretical analysis and computational methods, students learn to characterize and mitigate noise in practical radio systems. Upon completion, students can analyze signal-to-noise ratios, design filters for noise suppression, and evaluate performance limits of radio receivers.
642: This course examines the fundamental physics governing semiconductor device operation, including band theory, carrier transport mechanisms, and junction physics. Students study p-n junctions, bipolar transistors, field-effect transistors, and optoelectronic devices through both theoretical analysis and practical problem-solving. The course covers carrier generation-recombination processes, drift-diffusion equations, and device characteristics under various operating conditions. Students develop the ability to analyze semiconductor device behavior using energy band diagrams, derive device equations from first principles, and predict performance parameters for circuit applications. Laboratory work reinforces theoretical concepts through measurements of device characteristics and simulation using semiconductor modeling software.
643: This course covers the design and implementation of automated experimental systems using modern control technologies and instrumentation. Students learn to integrate hardware components, sensors, and data acquisition systems with software control platforms, including programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and real-time operating systems. The course emphasizes practical applications in physics and engineering experiments, teaching students to develop automated measurement protocols, process experimental data, and troubleshoot system failures. Through laboratory work, students gain hands-on experience with industrial automation tools, signal processing, and feedback control mechanisms. Upon completion, students can design, program, and maintain automated experimental setups for scientific research and industrial applications.
644: This course examines the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics and their applications to atomic and subatomic systems. Students study wave-particle duality, the Schrödinger equation, quantum operators, and the probabilistic interpretation of quantum states, with emphasis on solving problems in one and three dimensions. The course covers atomic structure, quantum numbers, the hydrogen atom, and multi-electron atoms using perturbation theory and variational methods. Students develop proficiency in mathematical techniques including linear algebra, differential equations, and eigenvalue problems essential for quantum mechanical calculations. Upon completion, students can apply quantum mechanical principles to analyze atomic phenomena and understand the theoretical foundations necessary for advanced courses in quantum field theory and condensed matter physics.
645: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles of radio engineering and oscillatory phenomena essential for radiophysics applications. Students study electromagnetic wave propagation, circuit analysis techniques, and the mathematical theory of oscillations including harmonic and damped oscillations. The course covers practical radio circuit components, resonance phenomena, and frequency response analysis using both analytical methods and computational tools. Through laboratory work and problem-solving exercises, students develop competency in designing simple radio circuits, analyzing oscillatory systems, and applying differential equations to model real-world electromagnetic behavior. Upon completion, students are prepared to advance to more specialized courses in antenna theory, signal processing, and communication systems.
646: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles of photonics, covering the generation, manipulation, and detection of light across the electromagnetic spectrum. Students study quantum properties of photons, optical materials and their interaction with electromagnetic radiation, and the design of optical systems including lasers, fiber optics, and photonic integrated circuits. The course develops practical skills in optical measurement techniques, laser safety protocols, and computational modeling of photonic devices using specialized software. Through laboratory work and problem-solving exercises, students learn to analyze light propagation in various media, design basic optical components, and apply photonic principles to telecommunications and sensing applications. Upon completion, students are prepared to work on optical system design projects and pursue advanced studies in photonics or related fields within radiophysics.
647: This course provides a rigorous foundation in single-variable calculus and real analysis, covering limits, continuity, differentiation, and integration of real functions. Students develop proficiency in computing derivatives and integrals, analyzing function behavior, and applying fundamental theorems of calculus to solve problems in physics and engineering. The course emphasizes both computational techniques and theoretical understanding, including epsilon-delta proofs and convergence criteria essential for advanced mathematics. Through problem sets and examinations, students master the analytical tools necessary for subsequent courses in differential equations, complex analysis, and signal processing within the radiophysics program.
648: This course covers the fundamental principles of electromagnetism, building on introductory electricity concepts to explore magnetic fields, electromagnetic induction, and Maxwell's equations. Students develop proficiency in analyzing electromagnetic phenomena using vector calculus, solving boundary value problems, and applying Faraday's law and Ampère's law to practical circuits and field configurations. The course emphasizes both theoretical understanding and computational problem-solving, with applications to electromagnetic wave propagation and radiation relevant to radiophysics. Through laboratory work and problem sets, students gain hands-on experience measuring magnetic properties, characterizing inductive and capacitive systems, and simulating electromagnetic fields using numerical methods. Upon completion, students can model complex electromagnetic systems, predict field behavior in various media, and apply these principles to design and analyze radiophysical devices and antenna systems.
649: This course covers the theory and applications of complex-valued functions, including analytic functions, Cauchy-Riemann equations, and complex integration. Students develop proficiency in evaluating contour integrals, applying the residue theorem, and performing Laurent series expansions to solve problems in electromagnetic theory and signal processing. The course emphasizes the connection between complex analysis and Fourier methods, essential for analyzing wave propagation and antenna design in radiophysics applications. Through problem sets and computational exercises, students gain the ability to apply complex analysis techniques to model and solve real-world engineering problems in their field.
650: Mathematical Analysis-3 continues the study of advanced calculus with emphasis on multivariable functions, vector analysis, and applications to physics and engineering problems. Students develop proficiency in partial derivatives, multiple integrals, line and surface integrals, and differential operators including gradient, divergence, and curl. The course covers Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem, and the divergence theorem, with applications to electromagnetic field theory and fluid dynamics relevant to radiophysics. Through problem-solving and computational exercises, students gain the ability to analyze complex physical phenomena modeled by multivariable functions and apply vector calculus techniques to real-world radiophysics scenarios.
651: This course provides hands-on experience in implementing fundamental computer science concepts through practical programming assignments and laboratory work. Students develop proficiency in multiple programming languages and paradigms while solving computational problems that reinforce theoretical knowledge from concurrent coursework. The practicum emphasizes algorithm design, data structure implementation, debugging techniques, and software development best practices using industry-standard tools and version control systems. Students complete individual and collaborative projects that demonstrate their ability to write efficient, well-documented code and analyze computational complexity. By course completion, students can independently develop functional software solutions, optimize code performance, and apply systematic problem-solving approaches to radiophysics-related computational challenges.
652: This course covers the fundamental principles of electrostatics and magnetostatics, including electric fields, potentials, and Gauss's law. Students develop proficiency in solving boundary value problems using analytical and numerical methods, with applications to conductors, dielectrics, and capacitive systems. The course introduces magnetic fields, Ampère's law, and the Lorentz force, establishing the foundation for understanding electromagnetic interactions. Through problem sets and laboratory work, students apply vector calculus and differential equations to model electric and magnetic phenomena relevant to radiophysics applications.
653: This course examines the microscopic foundations of thermodynamics through molecular physics principles, covering kinetic theory of gases, molecular motion, and statistical mechanics. Students develop proficiency in applying fundamental equations of state, analyzing thermodynamic processes, and calculating macroscopic properties from molecular behavior using computational methods. The course integrates laboratory work and numerical simulations to investigate heat transfer, phase transitions, and entropy, enabling students to model real physical systems and solve engineering problems in thermal management and energy conversion. By course completion, students can predict thermodynamic behavior of materials, design thermal systems, and apply statistical approaches to complex physical phenomena relevant to radiophysics applications.
654: This course builds on foundational programming concepts to develop intermediate software development skills using object-oriented programming principles and advanced data structures. Students learn to design and implement programs using languages such as C++ or Java, covering topics including classes, inheritance, polymorphism, dynamic memory management, and standard library containers. The course emphasizes algorithm design, code optimization, and debugging techniques through practical laboratory work and project-based assignments. By course completion, students can develop modular, efficient applications for scientific computing and embedded systems relevant to radiophysics applications.
655: Mathematical Analysis-2 continues the study of calculus with emphasis on multivariable functions, integration techniques, and series expansions. Students learn partial derivatives, multiple integrals, line and surface integrals, and their applications to physics and engineering problems. The course covers convergence of infinite series, power series, and Fourier series, providing essential mathematical foundations for signal processing and electromagnetic theory. Through problem-solving and rigorous proofs, students develop the analytical skills necessary for advanced courses in radiophysics and computational methods. Upon completion, students can apply multivariable calculus to model physical phenomena and analyze complex mathematical structures encountered in radiophysics applications.
656: This course equips students with systematic approaches to designing and conducting scientific research within radiophysics and computer technology domains. Students learn research methodologies including hypothesis formulation, experimental design, data collection protocols, and statistical analysis techniques essential for empirical investigations. The course covers literature review strategies, research ethics, and documentation standards while introducing students to relevant software tools for data analysis and visualization. Students develop competency in planning research projects, identifying appropriate methodologies for specific problems, and presenting findings in academic formats. By course completion, students are prepared to independently design feasible research proposals and execute investigations that meet scientific rigor standards.
657: This course covers the foundational principles of classical mechanics essential for radiophysics and computer technology applications. Students study kinematics, dynamics, energy conservation, momentum, rotational motion, and oscillatory systems through both theoretical frameworks and mathematical formalism. The course emphasizes vector analysis, differential equations, and problem-solving techniques applied to mechanical systems relevant to electromagnetic wave propagation and signal processing. Laboratory work includes experimental verification of mechanical principles and data analysis using computational tools. Upon completion, students can analyze mechanical phenomena quantitatively, apply conservation laws to complex systems, and connect mechanical principles to electromagnetic and computational contexts.
658: This course introduces students to core programming concepts and procedural programming paradigms using C/C++ as the primary language. Students learn fundamental constructs including variables, data types, control flow, functions, arrays, and pointers, while developing problem-solving skills through algorithmic thinking. The course emphasizes practical implementation through hands-on coding exercises and projects that reinforce theoretical concepts. Upon completion, students are able to write, debug, and optimize basic programs, understand memory management principles, and apply structured programming techniques to solve computational problems relevant to radiophysics applications.
659: This course covers the design and implementation of digital systems using programmable logic devices and microcontrollers. Students learn hardware description languages (HDL) such as VHDL or Verilog to model and simulate digital circuits, as well as embedded C/C++ programming for microcontroller applications. The course combines theoretical foundations in digital logic with practical laboratory work using field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and development boards. Students develop competency in circuit synthesis, timing analysis, and debugging of programmable systems, enabling them to design real-time embedded applications and reconfigurable hardware solutions.
660: Students engage in supervised practical work in research laboratories, industrial facilities, or technology companies specializing in radiophysics and electromagnetic systems. The course develops hands-on competency in experimental design, measurement techniques, signal processing, and data analysis using industry-standard instrumentation and software tools. Participants apply theoretical knowledge from core radiophysics courses to real-world problems involving antenna design, microwave systems, or wireless communications. Upon completion, students demonstrate proficiency in technical documentation, laboratory safety protocols, and collaborative problem-solving within professional engineering environments.
661: This course examines the foundational principles and practical applications of artificial intelligence systems within the context of radiophysics and computational technologies. Students study machine learning algorithms, neural networks, natural language processing, and knowledge representation techniques, with emphasis on signal processing applications relevant to radiophysics. The course covers programming implementations using Python and popular AI frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch, enabling students to develop and train intelligent systems. Through hands-on projects, students learn to design AI solutions for pattern recognition, classification, and prediction tasks in electromagnetic signal analysis and data interpretation. Upon completion, students are capable of building, evaluating, and deploying AI systems for complex problem-solving in radiophysics applications.
662: This course covers the fundamental principles of digital logic design and microprocessor architecture essential to modern computing systems. Students study Boolean algebra, logic gates, combinational and sequential circuits, and learn to design digital systems using hardware description languages (HDL) such as VHDL or Verilog. The course examines microprocessor organization, instruction sets, CPU design, memory hierarchies, and input/output systems through both theoretical analysis and practical implementation. Students gain hands-on experience with digital design tools, simulation software, and programmable logic devices (FPGAs) to prototype and test circuits. Upon completion, students can design and analyze digital logic circuits, understand processor operation at the architectural level, and implement solutions using modern digital design methodologies.
663: This course examines the architecture, protocols, and applications of Internet of Things (IoT) systems within embedded and networked environments. Students study wireless communication standards (WiFi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, LoRaWAN), sensor technologies, microcontroller programming, and cloud integration platforms for IoT deployments. The course covers practical implementation of IoT solutions including data acquisition, real-time processing, and remote monitoring systems using platforms such as Arduino, Raspberry Pi, and popular IoT frameworks. Students develop hands-on projects that integrate hardware sensors, communication modules, and software backends to create functional IoT applications in domains such as smart homes, industrial automation, and environmental monitoring. Upon completion, students can design, prototype, and deploy IoT systems with appropriate hardware-software integration and network connectivity.
664: This course examines the fundamental principles and architecture of mobile communication networks, from cellular systems to modern wireless technologies. Students study signal propagation, modulation techniques, multiple access schemes (FDMA, TDMA, CDMA), and network protocols essential to mobile systems operation. The course covers both theoretical foundations and practical applications, including hands-on work with software-defined radio tools and network simulation platforms. Upon completion, students can analyze mobile network performance, design basic cellular system components, and evaluate emerging technologies such as 4G/5G standards and their technical specifications.
665: This course examines the design and simulation of modern telecommunication systems using computational modeling techniques. Students learn to analyze signal propagation, modulation schemes, channel characteristics, and noise effects through mathematical modeling and software-based simulations. The course covers fundamental concepts in digital communications, including error correction codes, equalization techniques, and system performance metrics, with practical implementation using MATLAB, Simulink, or equivalent simulation tools. Students develop the ability to model end-to-end communication systems, predict system behavior under various conditions, and optimize performance parameters. By course completion, students can design, simulate, and evaluate telecommunication systems for real-world applications in wireless, optical, and wired networks.
666: This course examines the propagation, generation, and manipulation of electromagnetic waves in the microwave frequency range, with emphasis on practical engineering applications. Students study waveguide theory, transmission line analysis, antenna design principles, and microwave circuit components including filters, couplers, and amplifiers. The course covers both analytical methods and computational electromagnetic simulation tools for modeling microwave systems and predicting their performance characteristics. Through laboratory work and design projects, students develop competency in measuring microwave parameters, constructing and testing microwave devices, and optimizing circuits for specific frequency bands and impedance requirements. Upon completion, students can analyze complex microwave systems, design functional microwave components, and apply electromagnetic principles to solve real-world communication and sensing problems.
667: This course examines computational methods for modeling physical phenomena at micro and nanoscales, where quantum and classical mechanics intersect. Students learn to implement numerical simulations using molecular dynamics, Monte Carlo methods, and finite element analysis to predict material properties and system behavior. The course covers discretization techniques, boundary conditions, and validation strategies while utilizing software tools such as COMSOL, LAMMPS, and custom Python-based solvers. Students develop proficiency in translating theoretical physics into executable code and interpreting simulation results against experimental data. By course completion, students can design and execute multi-scale simulations for semiconductor devices, nanostructures, and metamaterials relevant to radiophysics applications.
668: This course provides hands-on training in designing and implementing automated experimental systems using modern control hardware and software. Students learn to interface sensors and actuators with microcontrollers and programmable logic controllers (PLCs), develop data acquisition systems, and write control algorithms in languages such as C/C++ and LabVIEW. Through practical laboratory exercises, students gain proficiency in real-time signal processing, system calibration, and troubleshooting of automated setups commonly used in physics and engineering research. By course completion, students can independently design, build, and debug automated measurement systems for scientific experiments in radiophysics and related fields.
669: This course examines the principles and implementation of digital communication systems, covering modulation techniques, channel coding, and signal detection methods. Students study fundamental concepts including pulse amplitude modulation (PAM), quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM), frequency shift keying (FSK), and phase shift keying (PSK), alongside error-correcting codes such as Hamming codes and convolutional codes. The course develops practical skills in designing and analyzing communication systems using MATLAB and simulation tools to model channel effects, noise, and interference. Students learn to calculate performance metrics including bit error rates (BER) and signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) for various modulation schemes. Upon completion, students can design digital communication systems, optimize transmission parameters for specific channel conditions, and evaluate system performance under realistic propagation scenarios.
670: This course examines the physics and engineering of semiconductor devices with emphasis on modern nanotechnology applications. Students study band theory, carrier transport mechanisms, and junction physics to understand device operation at both macro and nanoscales. The course covers fabrication techniques including lithography, etching, and deposition methods used in semiconductor manufacturing and nanosensor development. Students gain practical experience with characterization tools such as scanning electron microscopy, atomic force microscopy, and electrical measurement systems to analyze device performance. Upon completion, students can design and evaluate semiconductor-based nanosensors for applications in environmental monitoring, biomedical sensing, and radiation detection.
671: This course examines the principles and applications of optoelectronic devices and renewable energy conversion technologies. Students study semiconductor physics, photovoltaic cells, light-emitting diodes, photodetectors, and laser systems, alongside solar, wind, and alternative energy generation methods. The course covers device fabrication, characterization techniques, and energy conversion efficiency analysis using both theoretical models and laboratory measurements. Students develop practical skills in designing optoelectronic circuits, simulating energy systems, and evaluating renewable energy feasibility for real-world applications. Upon completion, students can analyze optoelectronic component performance, design sustainable energy solutions, and apply computational tools to optimize renewable energy systems.
672: This course examines the fundamental principles and practical techniques for synthesizing crystalline materials across multiple scales, from bulk crystals to nanometer-scale structures. Students study growth methods including Czochralski and Bridgman techniques for volumetric crystals, physical and chemical vapor deposition for thin films, and sol-gel, molecular beam epitaxy, and hydrothermal synthesis for nanostructures. The course covers process parameters such as temperature control, pressure management, precursor selection, and substrate preparation, with emphasis on how these variables influence crystal quality, defect formation, and material properties. Students gain hands-on experience with characterization techniques including X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and optical spectroscopy to evaluate grown materials. Upon completion, students can design and optimize growth protocols for specific applications in semiconductors, photonics, and advanced materials relevant to radiophysics and computational device development.
673: This course examines the fundamental physics, engineering principles, and manufacturing technologies underlying composite materials used in modern applications. Students study the structure-property relationships of fiber-reinforced polymers, ceramic matrix composites, and metal matrix composites, including stress transfer mechanisms, failure modes, and anisotropic behavior. The course covers fabrication techniques such as hand lay-up, vacuum infusion, filament winding, and automated fiber placement, alongside characterization methods including mechanical testing, microscopy, and non-destructive evaluation. Students develop competency in composite design calculations, laminate theory, and failure prediction using analytical and computational approaches. Upon completion, students can select appropriate composite materials for engineering applications, design composite structures, and troubleshoot manufacturing and performance issues in composite systems.
674: This course covers the fundamental principles and practical applications of microelectronic device design and integrated circuit fabrication. Students study semiconductor physics, transistor operation, logic gate design, and layout techniques for VLSI systems using industry-standard CAD tools such as Cadence and SPICE simulation software. The course emphasizes both analog and digital circuit design methodologies, including timing analysis, power consumption optimization, and design rule compliance. Through hands-on projects, students design and simulate functional circuits at the transistor and gate levels, developing competency in schematic capture, physical layout, and verification processes. Upon completion, students are able to design basic integrated circuits, analyze circuit performance through simulation, and understand the constraints imposed by manufacturing processes.
675: This course covers the fundamental principles and methodologies for modeling integrated circuits at various levels of abstraction. Students learn circuit simulation techniques, device physics modeling, and behavioral description languages such as VHDL and Verilog, with emphasis on SPICE-based simulation tools. The course addresses parasitic effects, noise analysis, and timing characterization essential for accurate IC performance prediction. Students develop practical skills in schematic capture, netlist generation, and post-layout simulation, enabling them to validate designs before fabrication. Upon completion, students can construct accurate computational models of complex integrated circuits and predict their electrical behavior under diverse operating conditions.
676: This course covers the theoretical foundations and practical aspects of wireless communication systems. Students examine electromagnetic wave propagation, modulation techniques, channel modeling, and signal detection methods essential for modern wireless networks. The course develops competency in analyzing link budgets, calculating path loss, and designing antenna systems for various frequency bands. Through laboratory work and simulations, students apply these principles to evaluate performance metrics such as bit error rate and spectral efficiency in wireless channels. Upon completion, students can design basic wireless communication systems and troubleshoot signal quality issues in real-world applications.
677: This course examines the principles of computer network architecture, protocols, and communication systems, with emphasis on the OSI and TCP/IP models. Students study network security threats, cryptographic algorithms, authentication mechanisms, and firewall technologies to protect data integrity and confidentiality. The course covers practical implementation of network security tools, packet analysis using Wireshark, and configuration of secure network protocols including SSL/TLS and VPN. Through hands-on laboratory work, students design secure network topologies, conduct vulnerability assessments, and implement access control policies. Upon completion, students are able to analyze network traffic, identify security vulnerabilities, and deploy appropriate countermeasures in modern computing environments.
678: This course provides students with foundational knowledge of radio and television transmission systems, covering electromagnetic wave propagation, modulation techniques (AM, FM, digital), and antenna theory. Students learn the principles of broadcast signal generation, transmission, reception, and processing using both theoretical analysis and practical laboratory work with RF equipment and software-defined radio platforms. The course examines the architecture of radio and television receivers, transmitters, and distribution networks, including modern digital broadcasting standards (DVB-T, DAB). Through hands-on experiments and simulations, students develop competency in signal analysis, circuit design, and troubleshooting of communication systems. Upon completion, students can design basic RF circuits, analyze transmission characteristics, and understand the technical infrastructure underlying contemporary broadcast media.
679: This practicum course provides hands-on experience in designing, implementing, and testing telecommunications systems and networks. Students work with industry-standard tools and equipment to configure transmission protocols, analyze signal propagation, and troubleshoot communication channels across various frequency bands. The course covers practical applications of modulation techniques, antenna systems, and digital signal processing in real-world telecommunications scenarios. Through laboratory exercises and projects, students develop competency in network performance measurement, spectrum analysis, and system optimization. Upon completion, students are able to independently design basic telecommunications links, diagnose system failures, and implement solutions for reliable data transmission.
680: This course examines the mathematical foundations and practical principles governing digital signal processing and discrete-time systems. Students study sampling theory, z-transforms, discrete Fourier transforms, and filter design techniques for both finite and infinite impulse response systems. The course covers signal quantization, spectral analysis methods, and the implementation of digital algorithms using computational tools and programming environments. Upon completion, students can analyze digital signals, design and implement digital filters, and apply signal processing techniques to real-world radiophysics and telecommunications applications.
681: This course teaches students to develop computational models for complex radiophysical phenomena using numerical methods and simulation techniques. Students learn to formulate mathematical representations of electromagnetic wave propagation, antenna systems, and signal processing problems, then implement solutions using programming languages such as MATLAB, Python, and specialized electromagnetic simulation software. The course covers finite difference time domain (FDTD) methods, method of moments (MoM), and other numerical approaches for solving Maxwell's equations in various media. Through practical projects, students gain proficiency in validating computational results against theoretical predictions and experimental data, preparing them to design and optimize radiophysical systems in telecommunications, radar, and remote sensing applications.
682: This course examines the design, analysis, and operation of radio technical systems used in communication, radar, and navigation applications. Students study electromagnetic wave propagation, antenna theory, signal modulation and demodulation techniques, and receiver/transmitter architectures. The course covers practical implementation using software tools for circuit simulation and signal processing, including MATLAB and specialized RF design software. Students develop competency in calculating system performance parameters such as gain, noise figure, and link budget, and apply these skills to design functional radio systems. Upon completion, students can analyze real-world radio technical systems, troubleshoot performance issues, and design basic communication and radar systems within specified technical constraints.
683: This course examines the principles and applications of microelectronic devices and circuits within the context of millimeter-wave and terahertz (GBH) technologies. Students study semiconductor physics, transistor design, and integrated circuit fabrication techniques specific to high-frequency applications, including field-effect transistors (FETs), heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs), and monolithic microwave integrated circuits (MMICs). The course covers circuit design methodologies, impedance matching, and noise analysis for GBH frequency bands, with emphasis on practical implementation in communication systems and sensing applications. Students develop competency in computer-aided design (CAD) tools for microelectronic simulation and layout, and gain hands-on experience analyzing and designing functional circuits operating at millimeter-wave frequencies.
684: This course covers the fundamental theory and practical applications of digital signal processing (DSP) in radiophysics and communications systems. Students learn discrete-time signal analysis, z-transforms, discrete Fourier transforms (DFT), and filter design techniques including FIR and IIR filter implementation. The course emphasizes hands-on experience with DSP algorithms using MATLAB and C/C++, enabling students to develop real-time signal processing applications for radar, wireless communications, and sensor data analysis. By course completion, students can design and implement digital filters, perform spectral analysis, and optimize signal processing pipelines for embedded systems and software-defined radio platforms.
685: This course examines the fundamental principles and industrial processes for manufacturing semiconductor materials and devices. Students study crystal growth techniques, doping methods, and purification processes essential for producing high-quality semiconductors, alongside the physics of p-n junctions, transistors, and integrated circuits. The course covers characterization techniques including X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and electrical measurements to evaluate material properties and device performance. Through laboratory work, students gain practical experience with semiconductor fabrication equipment, testing procedures, and quality control methods. Upon completion, students can design basic semiconductor devices, analyze material defects, and apply manufacturing technologies relevant to modern microelectronics and optoelectronics applications.
686: This course examines the fundamental physical principles governing semiconductor materials and devices. Students study band theory, charge carrier dynamics, and the physics of p-n junctions, including drift-diffusion processes and recombination mechanisms. The course covers semiconductor device operation including diodes, transistors, and integrated circuits, with emphasis on how microscopic physical phenomena determine macroscopic device characteristics. Through theoretical analysis and computational modeling, students develop the ability to predict semiconductor behavior under various operating conditions and design basic semiconductor circuits. Laboratory work reinforces theoretical concepts through measurements of semiconductor properties and device characterization.
687: This course examines the theoretical foundations and computational methods for modeling electromagnetic phenomena across various frequency ranges and media. Students learn to formulate Maxwell's equations in different coordinate systems, apply numerical techniques such as the finite difference time domain (FDTD) method and finite element method (FEM), and implement simulations using specialized software packages. The course covers wave propagation, scattering, antenna radiation patterns, and electromagnetic field interactions with materials. Through practical laboratory work, students develop proficiency in designing and validating electrodynamic simulations, analyzing results, and optimizing electromagnetic systems for engineering applications.
688: This course examines the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of secure communication systems within modern information networks. Students study cryptographic algorithms, including symmetric and asymmetric encryption methods, digital signatures, and authentication protocols, alongside their mathematical underpinnings in number theory and abstract algebra. The course covers key distribution mechanisms, secure channel establishment, and vulnerability analysis in communication protocols, with emphasis on real-world applications in network security and data protection. Through laboratory work, students implement cryptographic systems using industry-standard tools and programming languages, developing proficiency in security protocol design and threat modeling. Upon completion, students can design and evaluate secure communication architectures, identify cryptographic weaknesses, and apply appropriate security solutions to protect information transmission in radiophysics and computing applications.
689: This course provides students with foundational knowledge of telecommunications systems and signal transmission principles. Students study modulation techniques, signal processing, transmission media, and network architectures essential to modern communication systems. The course covers analog and digital modulation schemes, including AM, FM, and PSK, alongside practical applications in wireless and wired communications. Through laboratory work and problem-solving exercises, students develop competency in analyzing signal characteristics, calculating channel capacity, and designing basic communication links. Upon completion, students are prepared to apply telecommunications principles in advanced courses and professional practice within radiophysics and computer technology fields.
690: This course examines the fundamental principles and architecture of computer networks, covering the OSI and TCP/IP reference models, network protocols, and data transmission techniques. Students study routing algorithms, switching mechanisms, network addressing schemes (IPv4 and IPv6), and transport layer protocols including TCP and UDP. The course includes practical laboratory work with network simulation tools and packet analysis software such as Cisco Packet Tracer and Wireshark, enabling students to configure network devices, troubleshoot connectivity issues, and analyze network traffic. Upon completion, students can design basic network topologies, implement network configurations, and diagnose network performance problems in real-world scenarios.
691: This course examines the fundamental principles of electron emission, transport, and interaction in vacuum and semiconductor devices. Students study thermionic emission, photoelectric effects, and electron beam dynamics, along with the physics of semiconductor junctions and their applications in rectifiers, transistors, and photodetectors. The course covers both theoretical foundations and practical device operation, including vacuum tube characteristics and solid-state device behavior under various operating conditions. Through laboratory work and problem-solving, students develop the ability to analyze electron transport mechanisms, design simple electronic circuits, and predict device performance in radiophysics applications. This foundational knowledge prepares students for advanced courses in microelectronics, vacuum electronics, and electromagnetic device design.
735: This course provides Computer Science students with the opportunity to pursue advanced, self-directed research or study in specialized areas of computer science under faculty supervision. Students work independently to explore topics not covered in standard curriculum offerings, such as emerging technologies, specialized algorithms, advanced systems design, or domain-specific applications. Through regular meetings with their faculty advisor, students develop research proposals, conduct investigations, and produce technical documentation or software artifacts demonstrating mastery of their chosen subject. This course cultivates skills in self-directed learning, technical problem-solving, and independent project management essential for graduate studies and professional computer science careers.
807: This course examines the principles and practices of environmental engineering, focusing on water quality management, air pollution control, and waste treatment systems. Students develop proficiency in environmental assessment methodologies, regulatory compliance frameworks, and design of treatment technologies including wastewater systems, air filtration, and solid waste management. The course integrates laboratory work and computational modeling to analyze environmental contaminants and evaluate remediation strategies. Students apply engineering principles to real-world environmental problems and develop solutions that balance technical feasibility with sustainability considerations. Upon completion, students are prepared to design and manage environmental systems that protect public health and natural resources.
814: This course examines the fundamental principles of heat transfer through conduction, convection, and radiation, with emphasis on steady-state and transient thermal analysis. Students develop proficiency in solving heat transfer problems using analytical methods, numerical techniques, and computational tools, including finite difference and finite element methods. The course covers thermal resistance networks, heat exchangers, and practical applications in mechanical and chemical engineering systems. Students apply theoretical concepts to design and analyze thermal systems, predict temperature distributions, and optimize heat transfer performance in industrial equipment and processes.
825: This course examines the principles and practices of efficient resource allocation across engineering systems and projects. Students learn quantitative methods for resource planning, scheduling, and optimization, including techniques such as linear programming, network analysis, and project management frameworks. The course covers cost estimation, budget control, labor allocation, and material management with emphasis on minimizing waste and maximizing productivity. Through case studies and computational tools, students develop practical skills in resource forecasting, constraint management, and decision-making under limited availability. Upon completion, students are able to design resource strategies for complex engineering projects and implement monitoring systems to ensure optimal utilization throughout project lifecycles.
826: This course examines renewable and alternative energy sources including solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, and biomass technologies. Students learn the fundamental physics and engineering principles underlying each energy conversion method, analyze system efficiency and performance metrics, and evaluate economic and environmental feasibility of alternative energy projects. The course covers practical applications through case studies, design calculations, and simulation tools for energy system modeling. Students develop competency in assessing energy demand, sizing renewable systems, and comparing alternative energy solutions against conventional power generation. Upon completion, students can evaluate the technical and economic viability of alternative energy implementations and design basic renewable energy systems for specific applications.
829: Students in Capstone 1 undertake a comprehensive engineering design project that integrates knowledge from across the Engineering Sciences curriculum. The course emphasizes problem formulation, feasibility analysis, and preliminary design development, requiring students to conduct literature reviews, perform calculations, and create technical documentation. Students apply project management methodologies, collaborate in multidisciplinary teams, and present their work to faculty and industry professionals. By the end of the course, students will have developed a detailed project proposal with clear objectives, design specifications, and implementation timelines that serves as the foundation for their Capstone 2 project.
916: This course explores advanced techniques for developing high-performance applications across distributed and parallel computing environments. Students learn to optimize code for multi-core processors, GPUs, and cluster systems using languages such as C++, CUDA, and OpenMP, while studying memory management, cache optimization, and algorithmic efficiency. The course covers profiling tools, performance benchmarking methodologies, and parallel programming paradigms including shared-memory and message-passing models. Through hands-on projects, students design and implement scalable applications for computationally intensive problems in scientific computing, data processing, and machine learning. Upon completion, students can architect efficient high-performance systems, identify performance bottlenecks, and apply optimization strategies to real-world computational challenges.
941: This course equips students with practical expertise in acquiring, processing, and analyzing geospatial data using contemporary GIS technologies and remote sensing methodologies. Students learn to work with multiple data sources including satellite imagery, aerial photography, LiDAR, and GPS/GNSS systems, applying preprocessing and quality assurance techniques to ensure data integrity. The course covers spatial analysis methods such as interpolation, classification, overlay analysis, and statistical modeling within GIS software environments. Students develop proficiency in open-source and commercial GIS platforms while learning to extract meaningful geographic information for urban planning, environmental monitoring, and infrastructure assessment applications. By course completion, students can design data acquisition workflows, execute complex spatial analyses, and produce cartographic outputs suitable for professional geospatial projects.
942: This course examines the principles and practices of creating digital maps using contemporary GIS software and cartographic design methodologies. Students learn to design, produce, and optimize thematic maps, choropleth maps, and interactive visualizations using tools such as ArcGIS, QGIS, and web-based mapping platforms. The course covers map projection systems, symbolization techniques, color theory, and generalization principles to ensure cartographic accuracy and visual clarity. Students develop proficiency in preparing geospatial data for publication, creating multi-scale map series, and designing maps for both print and digital distribution. Upon completion, students are able to produce professional-quality digital cartographic products that effectively communicate spatial information to diverse audiences.
943: This course examines the principles and practices of cartographic design within geographic information systems environments. Students learn to create effective maps using GIS software, mastering techniques for data visualization, symbol design, color theory, and map composition. The course covers cartographic representation methods for various data types, including raster and vector data, and explores how to communicate spatial information clearly to diverse audiences. Students develop proficiency in GIS cartography tools and produce publication-ready maps for professional and academic applications. Upon completion, students are able to design, critique, and produce cartographically sound maps that effectively convey spatial relationships and geographic phenomena.
944: This course provides comprehensive instruction in Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) technology and its applications within geographic information systems. Students learn the fundamental principles of satellite positioning, signal processing, error sources, and correction techniques including differential GPS and real-time kinematic (RTK) methods. The course covers practical operation of GNSS receivers, field data collection protocols, and quality assurance procedures for spatial data acquisition. Students develop proficiency in processing raw GNSS observations, performing accuracy assessment, and integrating positioning data into GIS workflows for surveying, mapping, and spatial analysis projects. Upon completion, students are capable of designing and executing GNSS surveys, troubleshooting positioning errors, and evaluating data quality for professional geospatial applications.
945: This course examines the design, implementation, and management of geographic information systems infrastructure at organizational and regional scales. Students learn to architect GIS networks, configure spatial databases, integrate multiple data sources, and establish data governance frameworks that support enterprise-level geospatial operations. The course covers server technologies, cloud-based GIS platforms, interoperability standards (OGC, ISO), and system security protocols essential for managing large-scale spatial datasets. Upon completion, students will be able to design scalable GIS infrastructures, deploy distributed geospatial systems, and implement standards-compliant solutions for complex spatial data management in professional environments.
946: This course equips students with advanced programming skills essential for developing custom GIS applications and spatial analysis tools. Students learn object-oriented programming principles using languages such as Python and C++, with emphasis on geospatial libraries and APIs including GDAL, OGR, and QGIS Python bindings. The course covers spatial data structures, algorithms for geometric operations, and integration of raster and vector processing workflows. Students develop practical applications for data manipulation, automated cartography, and spatial problem-solving, preparing them to build scalable GIS solutions for real-world geographic challenges.
947: This course covers the principles and techniques of digital photography as applied to geospatial data collection and documentation. Students learn camera fundamentals, sensor technology, image acquisition workflows, and post-processing methods using industry-standard software such as Adobe Lightroom and Photoshop. The course emphasizes the integration of digital photography with GIS workflows, including georeferencing, orthorectification, and the use of aerial and terrestrial imagery for spatial analysis and mapping projects. Students develop practical skills in capturing, processing, and managing high-resolution imagery for architectural documentation, urban planning, and environmental monitoring applications. Upon completion, students can produce publication-quality geospatial imagery and integrate photographic data into comprehensive GIS projects.
948: This course examines the integration of Geographic Information Systems with Building Information Modelling technologies to create comprehensive spatial and structural datasets. Students learn to work with BIM software platforms, coordinate geospatial data with building-level information, and develop workflows that bridge GIS and BIM environments. The course covers data interoperability standards, 3D spatial analysis, and the technical challenges of merging multi-scale information systems. Students develop practical skills in managing complex datasets, performing spatial queries across integrated platforms, and creating decision-support tools for urban planning and facility management. Upon completion, students are able to design and implement integrated GIS-BIM solutions for large-scale construction projects and urban development initiatives.
949: This course equips students with theoretical foundations and practical skills in remote sensing technology and digital image processing techniques essential for geospatial analysis. Students learn to acquire, process, and interpret multispectral and hyperspectral satellite imagery using industry-standard software such as ENVI, ERDAS Imagine, and open-source tools like QGIS and Python libraries. The curriculum covers image preprocessing, atmospheric correction, radiometric calibration, classification algorithms (supervised and unsupervised), change detection, and spectral analysis methods. Students develop competency in extracting meaningful geospatial information from remotely sensed data for applications including land use/land cover mapping, urban planning, environmental monitoring, and infrastructure assessment. Through hands-on projects and case studies, students apply remote sensing workflows to real-world problems relevant to Armenia's geographic and development contexts.
950: This course equips students with the theoretical foundations and practical skills necessary to interpret and analyze radar imagery for geographic and environmental applications. Students learn the principles of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) systems, including signal processing, image formation, and the physical basis of radar backscatter from various terrain and land cover types. The course covers preprocessing techniques, radiometric and geometric corrections, and advanced interpretation methods for extracting spatial information from radar data. Through hands-on exercises using industry-standard software, students develop competency in decoding radar signatures, detecting surface changes, and integrating radar data with other geospatial datasets for mapping and monitoring applications. Upon completion, students are able to independently process radar imagery, interpret complex radar scenes, and apply radar remote sensing to solve real-world problems in urban planning, infrastructure assessment, and natural resource management.
951: This course provides students with advanced statistical methods for analyzing spatially distributed data and modeling spatial variability in geographic phenomena. Students learn fundamental geostatistical concepts including variography, kriging interpolation techniques (ordinary, universal, and co-kriging), and spatial autocorrelation analysis using industry-standard software such as ArcGIS, QGIS, and R/Python geostatistical libraries. The course covers both theoretical foundations and practical applications in environmental monitoring, natural resource assessment, and urban planning contexts relevant to geographic information systems. Students develop competency in constructing semivariograms, validating spatial models through cross-validation, and producing uncertainty estimates for spatial predictions. Upon completion, students are able to design and execute geostatistical analyses for real-world spatial datasets and communicate results through maps and statistical visualizations.
952: This course equips students with the technical skills to develop web-based geographic information systems using modern web technologies and GIS frameworks. Students learn to integrate mapping libraries (such as Leaflet, OpenLayers, and Mapbox), server-side GIS processing tools, and spatial databases to create interactive web applications. The course covers client-server architecture, RESTful APIs for geospatial data, and real-time data visualization techniques. Students develop practical experience with web mapping platforms, implement spatial queries, and deploy functional web GIS applications that serve diverse user needs in urban planning, environmental monitoring, and resource management.
953: This course examines the philosophical foundations and epistemological principles underlying geographic information science and spatial research. Students engage with scientific methodology, research design frameworks, and quantitative and qualitative approaches specific to GIS-based investigations. The course covers hypothesis formulation, data collection protocols, statistical analysis methods, and spatial analysis techniques essential for conducting rigorous geographic research. Students develop critical evaluation skills for assessing existing GIS research and design original research projects that integrate theoretical concepts with practical spatial analysis. Upon completion, students are prepared to conduct independent research, publish findings in peer-reviewed venues, and contribute to advancing GIS theory and practice.
954: This practice course provides students with hands-on experience in applying geographic information systems (GIS) methodologies to real-world spatial problems within architecture and construction contexts. Students work with industry-standard GIS software including ArcGIS, QGIS, and spatial analysis tools to process, analyze, and visualize geospatial data relevant to urban planning, site assessment, and infrastructure development. Through practical projects, students develop proficiency in data collection, geodatabase management, cartographic representation, and spatial modeling techniques essential for professional GIS practice. The course emphasizes the integration of GIS with architectural and construction workflows, enabling students to solve complex spatial challenges in project planning and site analysis. Upon completion, students are prepared to apply GIS technologies independently in professional settings within the architecture and construction industries.
955: This course equips students with essential project management methodologies and practices tailored to GIS-based initiatives and spatial data projects. Students learn to apply frameworks such as PMBOK, Agile, and Waterfall approaches while managing scope, schedule, budget, and resources specific to geospatial technology implementations. The course covers risk assessment, stakeholder communication, team coordination, and quality assurance within the context of GIS infrastructure development and spatial analysis projects. Students develop competencies in project planning tools, progress monitoring, and adaptive management strategies to deliver GIS solutions effectively in real-world organizational and construction-related environments. Upon completion, students are prepared to lead multidisciplinary teams and oversee complex geospatial projects from conception through implementation and evaluation.
956: Students undertake independent research under the guidance of a faculty supervisor to develop and complete a master's thesis in geographic information systems. The course encompasses all stages of thesis development, including research design, data collection and analysis using GIS software and spatial analysis techniques, and scholarly writing. Students apply advanced GIS methodologies, remote sensing, spatial modeling, and cartographic visualization to address original research questions in urban planning, environmental management, infrastructure analysis, or related geospatial domains. Upon completion, students present and defend their thesis before an academic committee, demonstrating mastery of GIS theory, technical proficiency, and the ability to conduct independent research at the graduate level.
957: This course examines fundamental mathematical and computational problems related to spherical geometry and its applications in computer science. Students study sphere equations, geometric properties, intersection algorithms, and computational methods for solving problems involving spherical surfaces and volumes. The course covers practical implementations using computational geometry libraries and programming techniques for 3D spatial analysis. Upon completion, students can model spherical objects, compute geometric relationships, and develop algorithms for sphere-based computational problems in graphics, physics simulations, and spatial data structures.
958: This course examines the principles and methodologies for designing, implementing, and managing enterprise-scale computer networks. Students study network architecture models, topology design, routing protocols, switching technologies, and quality of service (QoS) mechanisms to optimize network performance and reliability. The course covers practical tools for network simulation, configuration, and monitoring, including hands-on experience with network devices and management software. Students develop competency in assessing organizational requirements, selecting appropriate network technologies, and creating comprehensive network designs that balance performance, security, and cost considerations. Upon completion, students are able to design scalable network infrastructures, troubleshoot complex network issues, and implement solutions aligned with business objectives.
959: This course examines the principles and practices of information security within modern computing systems and networks. Students study cryptographic algorithms, authentication mechanisms, access control models, and threat analysis methodologies to design and implement secure systems. The course covers both theoretical foundations of security protocols and practical applications using industry-standard tools for vulnerability assessment, penetration testing, and security auditing. Students develop competency in identifying security risks, implementing defensive measures, and responding to security incidents in organizational environments. Upon completion, students are able to architect secure information systems, evaluate security vulnerabilities, and develop comprehensive security policies for enterprise infrastructure.
