960: This course examines the principles and methodologies for designing, analyzing, and maintaining reliable computer systems and software. Students study fault tolerance mechanisms, redundancy strategies, failure detection and recovery techniques, and reliability metrics including availability, mean time between failures (MTBF), and mean time to recovery (MTTR). The course covers formal verification methods, testing strategies for critical systems, and practical tools for system monitoring and diagnostics. Students apply these concepts to real-world scenarios involving distributed systems, databases, and mission-critical applications, developing the ability to architect systems that meet specified reliability requirements and minimize downtime.
961: This course examines the theoretical foundations and practical methodologies of system analysis and operational investigation within complex computational and organizational environments. Students learn to model system behavior, identify performance bottlenecks, and conduct empirical investigations using quantitative and qualitative research methods. The course covers system decomposition techniques, data collection and analysis protocols, simulation tools, and statistical methods for evaluating system efficiency and reliability. Students develop competency in designing experiments, interpreting operational metrics, and producing technical documentation that informs system optimization decisions. Upon completion, students can independently analyze large-scale systems, propose evidence-based improvements, and communicate findings to technical and non-technical stakeholders.
962: This course examines fundamental algorithm design paradigms and their theoretical foundations, including divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, greedy algorithms, and graph algorithms, with emphasis on complexity analysis and correctness proofs. Students study object-oriented software design principles, design patterns, and architectural patterns essential for building scalable, maintainable systems. The course integrates algorithmic problem-solving with OOP implementation, requiring students to apply theoretical concepts through practical programming projects in languages such as Java or C++. Students develop proficiency in analyzing algorithm efficiency, selecting appropriate data structures, and implementing robust object-oriented solutions to computational problems. Upon completion, students can design efficient algorithms, apply OOP principles to real-world software development, and evaluate trade-offs between algorithmic approaches and architectural decisions.
963: This course examines the architecture, design, and optimization of high-performance computing systems used in scientific and engineering applications. Students study parallel processing paradigms, distributed memory systems, GPU computing, and performance analysis techniques, working with tools such as MPI, OpenMP, and CUDA. The course covers computational bottlenecks, memory hierarchies, scalability metrics, and load balancing strategies essential for developing efficient large-scale applications. Through practical projects, students implement parallel algorithms, benchmark system performance, and optimize code for multi-core and heterogeneous computing environments. Upon completion, students can design and deploy high-performance solutions for computationally intensive problems in architecture, construction simulation, and scientific computing.
964: This course equips students with comprehensive knowledge of project management methodologies and practices essential for leading software development and IT infrastructure projects. Students learn to apply frameworks such as Agile, Scrum, Waterfall, and PRINCE2, alongside tools for scheduling, resource allocation, risk management, and stakeholder communication. The course covers project lifecycle phases including initiation, planning, execution, monitoring, and closure, with emphasis on managing scope, time, budget, and quality constraints. Students develop practical skills in using project management software such as Microsoft Project, Jira, and Asana to track deliverables and coordinate team activities. Upon completion, students are prepared to manage complex IT and construction-related projects, lead cross-functional teams, and make data-driven decisions to ensure project success within organizational and technical constraints.
965: This course provides advanced instruction in microcontroller architecture, design, and embedded systems programming. Students study processor organization, memory management, interrupt handling, and peripheral interfacing while developing proficiency with industry-standard microcontroller platforms such as ARM Cortex-M and AVR architectures. The course covers low-level programming in C and assembly language, real-time operating systems, and hardware-software integration techniques. Students design and implement embedded applications including sensor interfacing, motor control, and communication protocols (UART, SPI, I2C). By course completion, students can develop efficient embedded solutions, optimize code for resource-constrained environments, and troubleshoot hardware-software interactions in microcontroller-based systems.
966: This course examines the philosophical foundations of scientific inquiry and the systematic methodologies underlying research in computer science and informatics. Students engage with epistemological principles, research paradigms, and the structure of scientific knowledge while developing competency in designing, conducting, and documenting rigorous research projects. The course covers quantitative and qualitative research methods, experimental design, data analysis techniques, and academic writing standards specific to computer science disciplines. Students learn to critically evaluate existing research, formulate research questions, and apply appropriate methodological frameworks to their own investigations. Upon completion, students are prepared to conduct independent research and contribute meaningfully to the scientific literature in informatics.
967: This course examines the principles and practices of designing, testing, and maintaining reliable software systems. Students study fault tolerance mechanisms, failure analysis, software testing methodologies, and quality assurance techniques essential for mission-critical applications. The course covers reliability metrics, defect prediction models, and formal verification methods, with practical application to real-world software projects. Students develop skills in implementing redundancy strategies, conducting root cause analysis, and applying industry-standard reliability tools and frameworks. Upon completion, students are able to design robust software architectures, establish comprehensive testing protocols, and evaluate system reliability under various operational conditions.
968: This course equips students with mathematical modeling techniques and computational methods for solving complex engineering problems. Students learn to formulate physical phenomena as mathematical equations, select appropriate numerical solution strategies, and implement solutions using industry-standard software packages such as MATLAB, ANSYS, and COMSOL. The curriculum covers finite element analysis, computational fluid dynamics, structural analysis, and optimization algorithms applied to real-world engineering scenarios. Through practical projects, students develop proficiency in translating engineering requirements into computational models, validating results, and interpreting numerical simulations. Upon completion, students can independently design and execute mathematical simulations for diverse engineering applications and critically evaluate computational results.
969: This course examines the architecture, design, and implementation of large-scale data processing systems used in modern computing environments. Students study distributed computing frameworks such as Hadoop and Spark, learning how to process massive datasets across clusters of machines while managing fault tolerance and data consistency. The course covers key concepts including MapReduce programming models, data partitioning strategies, and NoSQL databases, alongside practical experience with data warehousing and real-time stream processing. Students develop proficiency in writing scalable data pipelines, optimizing query performance, and analyzing system trade-offs between latency, throughput, and resource utilization. Upon completion, students can architect and deploy big data solutions for complex analytical and operational workloads in enterprise environments.
970: This course equips students with practical expertise in contemporary artificial intelligence software frameworks and libraries essential for developing intelligent systems. Students learn to implement machine learning algorithms, neural networks, and deep learning models using industry-standard tools such as TensorFlow, PyTorch, scikit-learn, and Keras. The course covers data preprocessing, model training, evaluation, and deployment techniques while emphasizing best practices in AI software development. Students develop proficiency in Python programming for AI applications and gain hands-on experience building, optimizing, and deploying AI solutions across various domains including computer vision, natural language processing, and predictive analytics. Upon completion, students are capable of selecting appropriate AI tools, implementing complex machine learning pipelines, and integrating AI components into production software systems.
971: This practice course provides students with hands-on experience applying theoretical knowledge from the Informatics program to real-world software development and computational projects. Students work on practical assignments involving algorithm implementation, software design patterns, database management, and system architecture under faculty supervision. The course develops proficiency in programming languages, version control systems, debugging techniques, and collaborative development workflows essential for professional practice. Through structured projects and code reviews, students gain competency in translating computational concepts into functional applications and solving complex technical problems. Upon completion, students are prepared to contribute effectively to software development teams and tackle industry-standard engineering challenges.
972: This course examines the principles and applications of computer-aided design (CAD) systems and automated design methodologies in architecture and construction. Students study parametric modeling, algorithmic design, and Building Information Modeling (BIM) technologies, learning to leverage computational tools for complex design optimization and documentation. The course covers software platforms such as Revit, Grasshopper, and AutoCAD, alongside programming approaches for automating design workflows. Students develop practical skills in creating intelligent design systems, managing large-scale architectural data, and implementing automation to improve design efficiency and accuracy. Upon completion, students can design and implement automated solutions for architectural and construction projects, integrating computational thinking with domain-specific design requirements.
973: This course examines the intersection of software engineering principles and market dynamics, equipping students with methodologies to develop commercially viable software products. Students learn to analyze market requirements, conduct competitive analysis, and translate business objectives into technical specifications using agile and lean development frameworks. The course covers product lifecycle management, user research techniques, pricing strategies, and go-to-market planning specific to software solutions. Through case studies and project work, students develop skills in stakeholder communication, requirements prioritization, and risk assessment in commercial software development. Upon completion, students are prepared to lead software projects that balance technical excellence with market viability and business sustainability.
974: Students engage in independent research and thesis development under the guidance of a faculty supervisor, culminating in the completion and public defense of an original research contribution. The course emphasizes advanced problem-solving methodologies, technical writing, and the ability to conduct rigorous investigation within a specialized area of computer science or informatics. Students develop proficiency in research design, literature review, experimental validation, and the presentation of findings to academic audiences. Through iterative feedback sessions with their supervisor, students refine their research methodology, implementation, and analytical approaches. Upon completion, students demonstrate mastery of their chosen research domain and the capacity to contribute novel insights to the field of informatics.
975: This course develops students' proficiency in modern Armenian language and cultivates effective communication skills essential for professional and academic contexts.
